ruststream-rdkafka is the Apache Kafka broker for RustStream, built on rust-rdkafka and librdkafka. The guides take a Kafka service from installation to production. Start with Getting started.
This section draws how Kafka works, where ruststream-rdkafka sits between Kafka and the RustStream runtime, and what that costs a service.
What ruststream-rdkafka costs on every message: throughput against the raw rdkafka client, and instructions and allocations of its code.

The first chart runs one scenario three ways on a real Kafka broker. Raw client drives a librdkafka consumer directly. Broker crate drives this crate's subscription with a loop of its own and no runtime. RustStream is the service a user writes, a #[subscriber] handler in an app. The first gap is what this crate costs over the client it wraps, and the second is what the runtime adds on top. Each loop is a bar from its best round to its slowest, with a dot at the best round and a notch at the median. The zero of the axis is the raw client's best round, and a dot right of zero is slower. A hollow dot is a loop whose difference from the raw client is smaller than the spread of the rounds. The table under the chart prints the best round with the median in parentheses. The two scenarios differ in what an ack means. Under auto-commit librdkafka stores the offset when it hands the record over, and an ack is advisory. Under Commit::Tracked every ack stores an offset, as Settlement draws.

The second chart counts what one message costs on the service's thread: instructions under callgrind and allocations under DHAT, in the steady state. Each scenario is a service on KafkaBroker against the same broker. The count includes the framework's dispatch, this crate's code and the librdkafka calls made on that thread. Fetching, the group protocol, producing and delivery reports run on librdkafka's own threads and are not counted. Cold start is what starting the service, joining the group and taking the first record cost once.

How ruststream-rdkafka measures itself: the three loops, the run on a real broker, the broker-bound arithmetic and the code count. The procedure is the framework's own (RustStream methodology), and this page states what it is on Kafka.

One process runs each scenario three times over, as three loops that differ in one thing: what carries the records. Raw client. An rdkafka StreamConsumer, driven directly: receive, decode, store the offset. Broker crate. This crate and nothing above it: the broker connects, the topic descriptor opens a subscription, and a loop pulls deliveries off its stream, decodes them and acks them. RustStream. The service a user writes: a #[subscriber] handler and the app around it. Everything else is equal across the three: the consumer properties, the consumer group, the commit mode, the place of the ack, the decode into the same struct, the payload bytes, the tokio runtime with four worker threads, and the binary. The body is 512 bytes of JSON. It decodes into a struct of two integer fields, so the decode allocates nothing and the number is about this crate rather than about the JSON parser.

A fresh topic and a fresh consumer group per run. The topic has one partition, and it is dropped after the run, so a run never sees what an earlier one left. The consumer joins first. The producer, on a client of its own, starts once the cluster reports the group's member. The window opens at the first delivery and closes when the last one is decoded, in all three loops. Joining the group and creating the topic are outside it. The message count comes from a probe, which measures the raw loop's rate, so a measured run lasts at least five seconds on any machine. The loops are interleaved: raw, crate, RustStream, three rounds. Each loop reports its best, median and worst round. A row is broker-bound when the raw client spent the run waiting on the socket. That is arithmetic: a probe times one metadata request and its answer, a second probe counts the requests librdkafka sends per delivery, and the row is flagged when their product reaches half the measured time per message. The round trip is published with the machine, so the arithmetic can be checked.

Each scenario of the cost chart is the service a user writes, on KafkaBroker against the same broker, built without the testing feature. A consumer group reads a topic of one partition, and another thread fills the topic before the measured region opens. Instructions come from callgrind and allocations from DHAT. A scenario runs over one delivery, then 1000, then 2000. The difference between the last two is the steady cost of a message, and the single delivery is the cold start. The broker is real, so a count moves between runs of one binary: how often the service's thread finds the queue empty and waits depends on timing. Across three runs, consume and batch agreed within a hundredth of a percent and the reply moved by 2.3 percent. So a run against a saved baseline fails on five percent more instructions in a scenario, where the core's limit is two. Allocations are held to a floor each scenario declares, on every run.

just bench The recipe starts the stand from docker-compose.test.yml, runs both comparison scenarios, stops the stand and rewrites docs/benchmarks/results.json. It takes about fifteen minutes and wants the machine to itself. It clears RUSTFLAGS, so the binary is not tied to the CPU it was built on. Both recipes build the benchmarks the way a release is built, with fat link-time optimization across crates, so the numbers describe the code a service ships. just bench-code The code count takes a minute or two and needs valgrind. just bench-code --save-baseline=main on main records a baseline, and just bench-code --baseline=main on a branch compares with it.
What the benchmark numbers of ruststream-rdkafka measure, and what they do not allow you to conclude.

The three loops of a row are comparable with each other, because they ran in one process, interleaved, on one broker. A row is not comparable with a row another broker crate publishes: the transports do different work per message. The broker runs on the same machine, on the loopback. With no network latency, the same cost per message is a larger share of the time than it would be against a cluster across a network. Read the percentage as an upper bound on what a deployed service pays. A broker-bound row is one where the raw client waited on the socket for most of the run. The work of the crate and the runtime then happens inside that wait, and the difference comes out near zero. That is a lower bound on the cost, not a measurement of it.

documents.t: An instruction count holds this crate's code, the runtime above it and the librdkafka calls made on the service's thread. It moves a little between runs, because the broker is real. The same count costs more time where it misses the cache, so a count is not a time. Every figure is the steady state, the difference between a run of 1000 deliveries and one of 2000. Starting the service, joining the group and the first allocations behind them are the cold start, paid once.

A row is one consumer reading one topic of one partition, a small body and a single-node cluster. It measures what a delivery costs inside this crate, not what Kafka can carry. A topic of several partitions, a pool of worker lanes and a transactional pipeline each answer a different question, and the comparison measures none of them. The code chart counts a batch handler and a reply on the same stand. The numbers are a snapshot of one machine on one day, with the build recorded beside them. They are measured again by hand, on a machine given to the run alone: the differences they show are smaller than the noise of a shared one.

A record with a key goes to the partition its key hashes to, so the records of one key keep their order. A record without a key goes wherever the producer's partitioner puts it. Each partition numbers its records from zero, and its offsets grow apart from the other partitions'. Order holds inside a partition and nowhere else. A record stays in the log until retention deletes it, whether anyone read it or not. A consumer group reads every record of the topic once. The group hands each partition to one of its members, so the members share the work. A second group reads its own copy of every record, and the two never affect each other. What a group has read is one number per partition: its committed offset, the record it resumes from. Kafka stores no per-record acknowledgement. The model is Apache Kafka's own (concepts and terms). How a group shares its partitions is on Groups, and how the client reads and commits on Consumer.

The librdkafka consumer fetches ahead on threads of its own, hands records out one poll at a time, and commits a stored offset on a timer. The librdkafka consumer: fetch threads, the local queue, the application's poll, the offset store and the commit timerrecordson hand-overor laterreadcommitlibrdkafka threadsApplicationKafka clusterpartition leaders, group coordinatorFetchassigned partitionsLocal queuefetched aheadAuto-commiton a timer,every 5 sPollthe next recordProcessthe recordOffset storein memory,a positionper partition The diagram as text librdkafka threads: Fetch assigned partitions; Local queue fetched ahead; Auto-commit on a timer, every 5 s Application: Poll the next record; Process the record; Offset store in memory, a position per partition Kafka cluster partition leaders, group coordinator → Fetch assigned partitions: records Fetch assigned partitions → Local queue fetched ahead Local queue fetched ahead → Poll the next record Poll the next record → Process the record Poll the next record → Offset store in memory, a position per partition: on hand-over Process the record → Offset store in memory, a position per partition: or later Offset store in memory, a position per partition → Auto-commit on a timer, every 5 s: read Auto-commit on a timer, every 5 s → Kafka cluster partition leaders, group coordinator: commit librdkafka fetches the records of the assigned partitions into a local queue before the application asks for them. queued.max.messages.kbytes (64 MiB) bounds that queue. When it is full, fetching for a partition pauses for fetch.queue.backoff.ms (one second). A poll takes the next record off the queue. rust-rdkafka's StreamConsumer does that through recv, an async call that is safe to cancel. The offset store is an in-memory position per partition. By default (enable.auto.offset.store) a poll stores the offset of the record it hands out, before the application has processed it. The dashed arrow is the other way: the application turns the automatic store off and stores an offset once the record is processed. A timer commits the stored positions every auto.commit.interval.ms (five seconds) while enable.auto.commit is on, and once more when the consumer closes. A crash loses what was processed since the last commit, and it is read again. Under the default store, a record stored on hand-over and not yet processed is skipped after a crash. The behaviour and the defaults are librdkafka's (offset management, configuration).

A consumer group hands each partition to one member, and a member joining or leaving moves partitions in a rebalance. A rebalance: a member joins, the coordinator moves a partition to it, and it resumes from the committed offsetMember 1CoordinatorMember 2joinrevokeassignReadsP0, P1, P2Joinsthe groupRebalance:a newassignmentP2 isrevokedReadsP0, P1Reads P2 fromthe committedoffsetA member that stops heartbeating for session.timeout.msleaves the group, and its partitions move the same way The diagram as text Member 1: Reads P0, P1, P2; P2 is revoked; Reads P0, P1 Coordinator: Rebalance: a new assignment; A member that stops heartbeating for session.timeout.ms leaves the group, and its partitions move the same way Member 2: Joins the group; Reads P2 from the committed offset Joins the group → Rebalance: a new assignment: join Rebalance: a new assignment → P2 is revoked: revoke P2 is revoked → Reads P0, P1 Rebalance: a new assignment → Reads P2 from the committed offset: assign The group coordinator is a broker of the cluster. When a member joins or leaves, it starts a rebalance and the group agrees on a new assignment. A partition taken from one member is revoked there and assigned to another, which resumes from the group's committed offset. Work the first member did after its last commit is read again by the second. A partition the group has never committed starts where auto.offset.reset says: the end of the log by default. A member that stops sending heartbeats for session.timeout.ms (45 seconds in librdkafka) is removed from the group. A member that does not take a new record for max.poll.interval.ms (5 minutes) leaves the group too. partition.assignment.strategy decides how a rebalance moves partitions. The eager strategies, range and roundrobin (librdkafka's default is both, range first), revoke every partition and assign them anew. cooperative-sticky moves only the partitions that change owner, and the rest keep flowing during the rebalance (KIP-429). The two families cannot mix inside one group. A consumer can also take partitions by name instead of joining the group protocol. It then never rebalances, and nothing moves its partitions. The defaults are those of librdkafka (configuration, consumer groups).

A Kafka transaction makes records written to several partitions, and the consumed offsets, visible together or not at all. A consume-transform-produce transaction: records and consumed offsets commit together, or an abort discards bothmarkers writtenon errorBeginon the transactional producerProducerecords to any partitionsSend the consumed offsetswith the group's metadataCommitthe transactionA read_committed readersees the records, and theoffsets count as committedAbort:records discarded,offsets unmoved,the input isread againOne transactional id belongs to one live producer:initializing it again fences the earlier one The diagram as text Begin on the transactional producer → Produce records to any partitions Produce records to any partitions → Send the consumed offsets with the group's metadata Send the consumed offsets with the group's metadata → Commit the transaction Commit the transaction → A read_committed reader sees the records, and the offsets count as committed: markers written Send the consumed offsets with the group's metadata → Abort: records discarded, offsets unmoved, the input is read again: on error One transactional id belongs to one live producer: initializing it again fences the earlier one A transactional producer is named by its transactional.id. It runs one transaction at a time. Records produced inside it land in the log at once, and the commit writes markers that make them visible. A reader at the read_committed isolation level, librdkafka's default, sees a transaction's records only after the commit and never after an abort. A reader at read_uncommitted sees them as they are written. The consumed offsets can join the transaction. Then the input positions move exactly when the output becomes visible, which is the consume-transform-produce shape of KIP-447. An abort leaves the offsets where they were, so the input is read again into a new transaction. A transaction open longer than transaction.timeout.ms (one minute) is aborted by the coordinator. A producer started with an id already in use fences the earlier one: that producer's next call fails. The defaults and the fencing rule are librdkafka's (transactional producer, configuration).

One subscription reads all its partitions through one consumer; workers(n, by_key) spreads the records over lanes keyed by partition. Without workers, one loop runs the handler for each record in turn, so every partition keeps its order and nothing runs side by side. workers(n, by_key) runs n lanes. A record goes to the lane its key hashes to, and a lane runs its records in order. The key is the record's partition by default (LaneKey::Partition), so a partition never spreads over two lanes and Kafka's order is kept. Lanes fewer than partitions serve several partitions each. LaneKey::RecordKey keys a lane by the record key instead. Records of one key keep their order, and one partition's keys run side by side. A record without a key has no lane key, and such records rotate over the lanes. Acks from parallel lanes arrive out of order. Under Commit::Tracked the committed offset still never passes a record that has not settled, as Settlement draws. A batch handler takes one record and whatever librdkafka has already fetched, up to the size the mount site names, so a batch is often smaller than that size.

The runtime connects the broker when the app starts. Connect fetches the cluster's metadata through a short-lived client built from the producer settings, within connect_timeout (30 seconds). An unreachable cluster or a producer property librdkafka refuses fails the start. Each subscription's descriptor resolves once, against the connected broker. A group subscription opens its consumer and waits until the group has assigned it partitions and the start of each is known, up to assignment_timeout (one minute). Until the runtime starts reading, the consumer keeps answering the group, so a rebalance does not wait for it. Shutdown marks the connection closed, then flushes what the producer still holds within flush_timeout (30 seconds). ClosedKafkaBroker reports the records the flush left behind. A consumer closes when its subscription is dropped: it leaves the group, and unless its subscription is transactional it commits its stored position on the way.

The way of one Kafka record through a RustStream service: the fetch queue, the delivery, the handler, the reply and the commit. The KafkaMessage holds it where librdkafka put it, together with a reference count on the consumer that owns that buffer. The body, the key and the headers are read from the fetch buffer and not copied, and the headers are converted only when something asks for them. The consumer stays open for as long as a delivery holds a record of it. The one record that is copied is the one a waiting stream resolves itself: when the queue was empty, the record the wait returns is copied out. The handler's reply is encoded into a buffer the dispatch loop reuses. The publisher lends those bytes to librdkafka, which copies them into its own queue, and the publish returns once the cluster has acknowledged the record. A reply that fails to publish settles the delivery with a retry. The delivery settles after the reply. What that does to the committed offset depends on the subscription's Commit mode, which Settlement draws.

What ack, drop, retry and retry_after become on Kafka, which commits one offset per partition instead of acknowledging records. Commit::Tracked on one partition: the stored position stops below the lowest delivery that has not settledstored atauto-commitOne partition, offsets as delivered10settled11settled12running13settled14settled15runningStored position: 11below the lowestrunning deliveryCommitted offset: 12the record the groupresumes fromWhen 12 settles,the position movesto 14: 15 is stillrunning The diagram as text Stored position: 11 below the lowest running delivery → 11 settled: stored at Stored position: 11 below the lowest running delivery → Committed offset: 12 the record the group resumes from: auto-commit One partition, offsets as delivered 10 settled 12 running 13 settled 14 settled 15 running When 12 settles, the position moves to 14: 15 is still running Kafka keeps one committed offset per partition and group. The subscription's Commit mode decides how a handler's outcome reaches it. Under Commit::Tracked, the crate turns librdkafka's automatic offset store off and records every offset it delivers. A settlement stores the position just below the lowest delivery still running, or the highest delivered offset once none is running. Acks from parallel lanes can arrive in any order, and the stored position never passes unfinished work. Offsets the consumer never receives, such as transaction markers or compacted records, do not hold it back. librdkafka's timer commits the stored position as usual. Outcome Commit::Auto (default) Commit::Tracked Commit::Transactional ack Nothing: librdkafka stored the offset when it handed the record over The offset settles and the stored position moves up The offset settles; the pipeline commits it with its next window drop Nothing, as for ack The offset settles, as for ack The offset settles, as for ack retry() Refused (AckError::Unsupported) and logged: nothing brings the record back The record is delivered again ahead of what is fetched next, and the position waits for it The open window cannot commit: it aborts and is read again A rebalance or a seek that moves a partition discards its tracked state. A settlement of a delivery read before the move changes nothing, because the partition's next reader starts from the committed offset anyway. Under Commit::Transactional the consumer commits nothing itself. The EosPipeline of the same id adds the settled positions to its producer transaction every commit_interval (100 milliseconds), so the consumed offsets and the published records become visible together, as Kafka transactions draws.

A KafkaTopic subscription reports its own topic. A KafkaTopics or KafkaPartitions subscription reads a set no single publish reaches, so its registration names the destination, or the app refuses to start. The parts of ruststream-rdkafka a Kafka service uses, one page per component: the broker (KafkaBroker), its subscriptions, its publish policies and the in-process transport a TestApp test runs on.

With the asyncapi feature the generated document speaks Kafka: the server, the topic behind each channel, the group of each operation. The core builds the AsyncAPI document from the app, before anything connects. This crate adds the specification's kafka binding, version 0.5.0, to the parts it knows about. A server reports the cluster's coordinates and its schema registry. A channel reports the topic behind it. A receive operation reports the consumer group it reads in. Everything comes from the service's own declarations: the broker, the descriptors and the destinations the mount sites resolved. The document is published and shared, so no binding carries a credential. The binary #[ruststream::app] writes prints the document with asyncapi gen.

The dependency line: ruststream-rdkafka = { version = "0.7", features = ["asyncapi"] } The service registers its broker under the label kafka, the key of its server in the document. cargo run --example kafka_asyncapi --features asyncapi,schema-registry -- asyncapi gen prints the document. Macros Manual examples/kafka_asyncapi.rs fn service(broker: KafkaBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "1.0.0")).with_broker_labeled("kafka", broker, |b| { b.include(confirm); b.include(audit); b.include(ledger); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let password = env::var("KAFKA_PASSWORD").unwrap_or_default(); service(broker(&password)) } examples/manual/kafka_asyncapi.rs fn service(broker: KafkaBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "1.0.0")).with_broker_labeled("kafka", broker, |b| { let confirm = subscriber("orders", Confirm).map_source(|_| orders()); b.include(confirm.reply().to("confirmations").build()); b.include( subscriber("audit", Audit) .map_source(|_| audit_topics()) .build(), ); b.include( subscriber("ledger", Ledger) .map_source(|_| ledger_partitions()) .build(), ); }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let password = env::var("KAFKA_PASSWORD").unwrap_or_default(); service(broker(&password)) }

Each channel reports its topic: the descriptor's for a subscription, the resolved destination for a publish. The channel binding has one field, topic. A subscription by name, a KafkaTopic and a KafkaPartitions reader each report the one topic they read. A KafkaTopics set or pattern reads several topics, so its channel carries no binding. A channel the service publishes to reports the topic the mount site resolved. That is a reply("dest") clause, a reply type's #[outgoing(name)], the name of a slot entry, or a declared dead-letter topic. A publish policy holds producer settings and no topic, so the policy itself adds nothing to the channel.

The channels orders and ledger report the topics their descriptors read, and confirmations the topic the reply clause names. The channel of the audit and audit.eu set reports none. Macros Manual examples/kafka_asyncapi.rs #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("orders") .group("orders-svc") .config("client.id", "orders-reader"), reply("confirmations") )] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { Confirmation { id: order.id } } #[subscriber(KafkaTopics::new(["audit", "audit.eu"]).group("audit-svc"))] async fn audit(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "audited"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[subscriber(KafkaPartitions::new("ledger", [0, 1]))] async fn ledger(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "booked"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_asyncapi.rs /// The topic `orders`, read in the group `orders-svc` by the client `orders-reader`. fn orders() -> KafkaTopic { KafkaTopic::new("orders") .group("orders-svc") .config("client.id", "orders-reader") } /// Both audit topics, through one consumer in the group `audit-svc`. fn audit_topics() -> KafkaTopics { KafkaTopics::new(["audit", "audit.eu"]).group("audit-svc") } /// The first two partitions of `ledger`, read apart from any group. fn ledger_partitions() -> KafkaPartitions { KafkaPartitions::new("ledger", [0, 1]) }

A receive operation reports the consumer group its descriptor names, and the client id its config sets. The operation binding carries groupId and clientId, each as a one-value schema. groupId is the group the descriptor names, such as KafkaTopic::group. The document is built before the broker connects, from the descriptor alone, so the broker's default_group does not appear. clientId appears when the descriptor's config sets client.id. An operation with neither carries no binding.

The operation receive_orders reports the group orders-svc and the client id orders-reader. Macros Manual examples/kafka_asyncapi.rs #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("orders") .group("orders-svc") .config("client.id", "orders-reader"), reply("confirmations") )] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { Confirmation { id: order.id } } examples/manual/kafka_asyncapi.rs /// The topic `orders`, read in the group `orders-svc` by the client `orders-reader`. fn orders() -> KafkaTopic { KafkaTopic::new("orders") .group("orders-svc") .config("client.id", "orders-reader") }

The server reports bare host:port coordinates and the schema registry, never credentials and never a protocol version. A broker registered with with_broker_labeled is a server of the document, under its label. Its host is the bootstrap servers, joined with commas. A PLAINTEXT:// or SASL_SSL:// prefix and any user info an address carries stay out of it. The protocol is kafka. protocolVersion stays out: a Kafka client and the cluster agree on a version per request type, so no one number describes what clients speak. A broker with a SchemaRegistry adds the server binding. schemaRegistryUrl is the registry's address without user info, and schemaRegistryVendor is confluent, the envelope this crate writes. The SASL password and the registry's basic-auth credentials stay out of the document.

The broker reaches two brokers over SASL_SSL and a registry with basic auth. Its server in the document is kafka-1.internal:9093,kafka-2.internal:9093 with the registry https://registry.internal:8081. Macros Manual examples/kafka_asyncapi.rs /// The production cluster over `SASL_SSL`, with its schema registry. fn broker(password: &str) -> KafkaBroker { let registry = SchemaRegistry::new("https://registry.internal:8081").basic_auth("orders-svc", password); KafkaBroker::new([ "SASL_SSL://kafka-1.internal:9093", "SASL_SSL://kafka-2.internal:9093", ]) .default_group("orders-svc") .config("security.protocol", "SASL_SSL") .config("sasl.mechanism", "SCRAM-SHA-512") .config("sasl.username", "orders-svc") .config("sasl.password", password) .schema_registry(registry) } examples/manual/kafka_asyncapi.rs /// The production cluster over `SASL_SSL`, with its schema registry. fn broker(password: &str) -> KafkaBroker { let registry = SchemaRegistry::new("https://registry.internal:8081").basic_auth("orders-svc", password); KafkaBroker::new([ "SASL_SSL://kafka-1.internal:9093", "SASL_SSL://kafka-2.internal:9093", ]) .default_group("orders-svc") .config("security.protocol", "SASL_SSL") .config("sasl.mechanism", "SCRAM-SHA-512") .config("sasl.username", "orders-svc") .config("sasl.password", password) .schema_registry(registry) }

AvroCodec::registry reads each delivery with its writer schema and frames each value with the id of its subject. AvroCodec is a codec, so a handler on it takes and returns ordinary serde structs. A model derives AvroSchema from apache-avro, which the crate re-exports as avro::AvroSchema. The codec is built from a SchemaPrefetch, and the same prefetch is attached to the broker with KafkaBroker::schema_prefetch. The codec itself is synchronous and reads only the prefetch's cache, so its encode and decode reach no network. Decoding needs no registration. The envelope of each delivery names the writer schema, the prefetch resolves it before the decode, and the codec reads the datum with it. One codec therefore decodes every record type that arrives on its topics. register::<T>(subject) is the publish side: values of T are framed with the id of subject. The codec finds the subject by the name serde gives the value's type. A value of a type that no one registered fails its publish, and the error names the type and lists the registered ones. Two registered types with one serde name stop the app at startup. The codec named with with_broker_codec decodes the deliveries of its scope. A reply names its codec at its own position, .out_reply(policy).codec(codec); a reply without one is encoded with the default codec. The codec and the transcode are alternatives on one broker: a broker with schema_registry hands every subscription plain JSON.

Receipt { id: delivery.id, delivered: true, } } fn app(registry: SchemaRegistry) -> impl App { // The prefetch resolves subjects at connect and each writer schema before its decode. let prefetch = SchemaPrefetch::new(registry); AvroCodec::local pins one schema and writes a bare datum, with no envelope, no registry and no I/O. The schema passed in is the one the wire carries: T::get_schema() when the model defines it, or a parsed .avsc file when the schema text is the source of truth. Every message is written and read with that schema, so producers and consumers of the topic agree on it outside the service. local returns an error when the schema refers to a name it does not define. The codec registers nothing; register belongs to the registry form. avro::encode and avro::decode are the same conversion as free functions, for a tool that works on datum bytes outside an app. Both use the type's own schema.

Macros Manual examples/kafka_avro_local.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, AvroSchema)] struct Reading { sensor: String, celsius: f64, } #[subscriber("readings")] async fn record(reading: &Reading) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(reading.sensor, reading.celsius, "reading recorded"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { // The schema the wire carries, pinned here; nothing reaches a registry. let codec = AvroCodec::local(Reading::get_schema()).expect("a derived schema resolves"); let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("readings-svc"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("readings", "0.1.0")).with_broker_codec(broker, codec, |b| { b.include(record); }) } examples/manual/kafka_avro_local.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, AvroSchema, JsonSchema)] struct Reading { sensor: String, celsius: f64, } /// The definition `#[subscriber("readings")]` would have minted. struct Record; impl Handle<Reading> for Record { fn handle( &self, reading: &Reading, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(reading.sensor, reading.celsius, "reading recorded"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { // The schema the wire carries, pinned here; nothing reaches a registry. let codec = AvroCodec::local(Reading::get_schema()).expect("a derived schema resolves"); let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("readings-svc"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("readings", "0.1.0")).with_broker_codec(broker, codec, |b| { b.include(subscriber("readings", Record).build()); }) } // What `#[ruststream::app]` writes: the command line on a multi-threaded Tokio runtime. fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) }

resolve_onto reads every delivery onto a reader schema, so Avro fills the fields the writer never wrote from their defaults. A datum read with its writer schema yields what the writer wrote. A consumer whose model has moved ahead of its producers names its own schema as the reader schema, and Avro's schema resolution fills each missing field from the default that schema declares. The model declares a default with #[avro(default = "..")], whose value is JSON. A field with no default that the writer never wrote fails the decode. The reader schema applies to decoding only; a publish still writes the schema the wire carries. On a local codec the pair is checked when the codec is built, so a reader schema that cannot resolve against the writer schema is an error at startup. On a registry codec the writer schemas arrive with the deliveries, so a pair that cannot resolve fails the decode that meets it. A codec carrying a reader schema reads one type, so a handler that needs one mounts it in a Router with with_codec, and the scope's codec serves the other handlers.

On a broker with schema_registry an Avro datum arrives as JSON, and SchemaFrame writes Avro where the reply's subject holds an Avro schema. The handler and its models stay on the default JSON codec and carry no Avro type. On the way in, the subscription reads the envelope, resolves the writer schema by its id and rewrites the payload as a JSON document. On the way out, the layer resolves the subject of the destination topic, {topic}-value, and writes the JSON payload as an Avro datum of that subject's schema, inside the envelope. The reply's model derives AvroSchema only to register its subject at startup with register_avro. The flow is the same as the JSON transcode; the subject's schema type decides the format on the wire. The transcode is the compatibility path for a service that keeps plain serde models on a registry-backed topic. Each message takes a hop through JSON. A datum is read with its writer schema alone, so a field the writer never wrote has no default to take; the codec with resolve_onto is the path that resolves schemas. An Avro type that JSON has no form for does not pass through the transcode.

KafkaBroker connects a service to a Kafka cluster; new only records the bootstrap servers, and the runtime connects it at startup. KafkaBroker::new takes the bootstrap servers, each a host or host:port the client starts from. It does no I/O, so the whole service fits the synchronous #[ruststream::app] builder. The settings that follow it are builder steps too: a default consumer group, librdkafka properties through config, and the startup and shutdown bounds. A property the service leaves unset keeps the librdkafka default. At startup the runtime connects the broker and receives a ConnectedKafkaBroker. The connect probes the cluster, so an unreachable cluster fails startup instead of the first publish. Every subscription and every publisher of the service opens against that connected form. At shutdown the runtime turns it into a ClosedKafkaBroker, after the producer has flushed what the handlers published. #[subscriber("orders")] reads the topic orders in the broker's default group. Kafka reads a topic only through a consumer group, so a subscription with no group of its own on a broker with no default group fails startup. The descriptors that set a group, several topics or exact partitions per subscription are on the Subscriptions pages.

The service reads the topic orders in the group orders-svc. cargo run --example kafka_quickstart --features testing -- run starts it against a cluster on localhost:9092. Macros Manual examples/kafka_quickstart.rs use ruststream_rdkafka::prelude::*; #[subscriber("orders")] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("orders-svc"), |b| { b.include(place); }, ) } examples/manual/kafka_quickstart.rs use ruststream_rdkafka::prelude::*; struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("orders-svc"), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Place).build()); }, ) }

config and producer_config pass any librdkafka property to every client of the broker or to its producer only. A property set with config reaches every consumer and the producer the broker creates. A property that applies to one side only is ignored by the other, as librdkafka ignores it. producer_config applies on top of config, to the producer alone: acks, compression.type, message.max.bytes, linger.ms. A descriptor's own config adds consumer properties for one subscription. The names and values are librdkafka's, listed in its CONFIGURATION.md. librdkafka checks every property when the broker connects. An unknown name or a value it refuses fails startup with KafkaError::Connect, so a typo never reaches the first publish. The in-process cluster a TestApp test runs on reads the same properties. It refuses what librdkafka refuses, and a record over the producer's message.max.bytes is refused there as on a cluster.

The broker names its clients orders-svc and compresses what it publishes. A shipment over 64 KiB is refused, and the order that produced it is settled as a retry. KafkaError is the one error type of the crate: connect, publish, consume, transactions, the registry and the wire format. Each variant names the step that failed. The librdkafka error behind it is its source, so the client library's types stay out of the crate's API. Variant When Connect the client could not be created, a property was refused, or the cluster did not answer the startup probe Subscribe a consumer could not be created or subscribed, or its group did not assign it partitions in time Consume an open consumer failed to receive Publish the cluster refused a record or did not confirm it, or the shutdown flush ran out of time Closed a publisher or a transaction was used after the broker shut down InvalidOptions the settings cannot work together, such as a subscription with no consumer group TransactionBusy, NoTransaction a transaction was begun twice on one publisher, or ended with none open SchemaRegistry, SchemaRegistryTimeout a registry request failed or went unanswered (schema-registry feature) WireFormat a value did not match its Avro or Protobuf wire form (schema-registry feature) A service meets the error in two places. A failed startup carries it as the source of the runtime's error, and the service exits before it reads anything. A publish from a handler returns it inside the core's PublishError, and the handler decides how the delivery settles. The enum is #[non_exhaustive], so a match on it ends with a wildcard arm.

A shipment the cluster refuses is logged with its cause, and the order is settled as a retry. Macros Manual examples/kafka_broker_errors.rs #[subscriber("orders")] async fn ship(order: &Order, Out(shipments): Out<impl Publisher, Shipments>) -> HandlerOutcome { let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id, labels: (1..=order.parcels) .map(|parcel| format!("{}-{parcel:05}", order.id)) .collect(), }; if let Err(err) = shipments.message(&shipment).publish().await { // The error names the topic and the cluster's reason. tracing::warn!(subscription = "orders", order.id, error = %err, "shipment not published"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_broker_errors.rs struct Ship; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Ship where Entry: OutEntry<Shipments, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id, labels: (1..=order.parcels) .map(|parcel| format!("{}-{parcel:05}", order.id)) .collect(), }; if let Err(err) = outs.get(Shipments).message(&shipment).publish().await { // The error names the topic and the cluster's reason. tracing::warn!(subscription = "orders", order.id, error = %err, "shipment not published"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } }

One glob, ruststream_rdkafka::prelude, brings the core prelude, the descriptors, the policies under concept names and the context keys. use ruststream_rdkafka::prelude::*; is the one import a Kafka service writes. It carries the core's own prelude, so #[subscriber], RustStream, HandlerOutcome and Out come with it. It adds KafkaBroker, the descriptors KafkaTopic, KafkaTopics and KafkaPartitions with their settings (Commit, StartOffset, Assignment, LaneKey), the reply transforms RoundRobin and ToSourceTopic, and the context keys Topic, Partition, Position, Source and SeekHandle. The publish policies come under the names every broker crate uses: Publish is KafkaPublish, TransactionalPublish is KafkaTransactionalPublish, PartitionedPublish is KafkaPartitionedPublish, and EosPublish is KafkaEosPublish. So a mount site reads the same on every broker. Two broker preludes in one file collide on these names; the prefixed types at the crate root tell them apart. A handler body bounds its slots with capability traits, such as Out<impl TransactionalPublisher>, and names no broker type. The one exception is a body that sets a per-record setting: partition(..) needs KafkaPublishSteps in scope and the slot bounded Out<impl Publisher<Options = KafkaOptions>, Marker>, both from this prelude.

The descriptor, its settings and the reply policy all come from the one glob. SASL and TLS are librdkafka properties set through config; the ssl and ssl-vendored features link the OpenSSL they need. security.protocol picks the listener: PLAINTEXT, SSL, SASL_PLAINTEXT or SASL_SSL. sasl.mechanism, sasl.username and sasl.password set the SASL login, and the ssl.* properties the certificates. The bootstrap servers are the addresses of the listener the protocol speaks to. On the default features, librdkafka carries one SASL mechanism, PLAIN. The ssl feature links the system OpenSSL, and ssl-vendored builds OpenSSL from source; either one adds TLS and the SCRAM-SHA-256, SCRAM-SHA-512 and OAUTHBEARER mechanisms. Without it, a TLS property fails startup with "OpenSSL not available at build time", and a SCRAM or OAUTHBEARER mechanism fails the connect. The zstd feature adds that compression codec; the other codecs are built in. A misspelled security.protocol fails startup, in a TestApp test as on a cluster. The generated AsyncAPI document reports the bootstrap addresses and never the credentials.

The dependency line: ruststream-rdkafka = { version = "0.7", features = ["ssl"] } The service authenticates with SCRAM over TLS and verifies the cluster against its own certificate authority. The password comes from the environment.
