Shutdown flushes in-flight publishes within flush_timeout, and a publisher used afterwards reports KafkaError::Closed. librdkafka sends records in the background, so a publish the cluster has not yet confirmed may still sit in the producer's queue. At shutdown the runtime closes the connection first and then flushes that queue. The flush waits up to flush_timeout, 30 seconds by default. Records still queued after it fail the shutdown with KafkaError::Publish. A service that never published has no producer and nothing to flush. A publisher taken before the shutdown keeps pointing at the closed connection. A publish through it, or a commit or an abort of its transaction, returns KafkaError::Closed with the topic or the transactional id, and never succeeds against the dead connection. A tool that drives the broker by hand receives a ClosedKafkaBroker from the shutdown; its unflushed_records is the number of records librdkafka still held.

The flush gets ten seconds, and the shipments the handler replied with reach the cluster before the service exits. Macros Manual examples/kafka_broker_shutdown.rs /// The cluster at `servers`; shutdown waits up to ten seconds for in-flight records. fn broker(servers: &str) -> KafkaBroker { KafkaBroker::new([servers]) .default_group("orders-svc") .flush_timeout(Duration::from_secs(10)) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("localhost:9092")) } examples/manual/kafka_broker_shutdown.rs /// The cluster at `servers`; shutdown waits up to ten seconds for in-flight records. fn broker(servers: &str) -> KafkaBroker { KafkaBroker::new([servers]) .default_group("orders-svc") .flush_timeout(Duration::from_secs(10)) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("localhost:9092")) }

Startup probes the cluster within connect_timeout and waits up to assignment_timeout for each group to assign its partitions. The connect fetches the cluster's metadata. A cluster that does not answer within connect_timeout, 30 seconds by default, fails startup with KafkaError::Connect. The connect also checks the producer's properties, and opens no producer: the first publish opens it, so a service that only consumes runs none. A subscription through a consumer group is open once the group has assigned this member its partitions and the offset each one starts from is known. From that moment everything published to the topic reaches it. Startup waits for each group up to assignment_timeout, 60 seconds by default, and then fails with KafkaError::Subscribe, naming the subscription and its group. A new group waits the coordinator's group.initial.rebalance.delay.ms, three seconds by default. A group that still holds a member which left without a word waits until that member's session.timeout.ms expires, 45 seconds by default. A subscription that names its partitions with KafkaPartitions joins no group and does not wait. A subscription to a topic the cluster does not have yet opens without partitions. When the topic appears, the group reads it from where auto.offset.reset puts it, the end of the log by default, so the record that created the topic is not read.

The probe gives up after five seconds, and each group gets twenty seconds to assign its partitions. Macros Manual examples/kafka_broker_startup.rs /// The cluster at `servers`, with both startup waits bounded. fn broker(servers: &str) -> KafkaBroker { KafkaBroker::new([servers]) .default_group("orders-svc") // The reachability probe: a metadata fetch. .connect_timeout(Duration::from_secs(5)) // Each consumer group assigning this member its partitions. .assignment_timeout(Duration::from_secs(20)) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { service(broker("localhost:9092")) } examples/manual/kafka_broker_startup.rs /// The cluster at `servers`, with both startup waits bounded. fn broker(servers: &str) -> KafkaBroker { KafkaBroker::new([servers]) .default_group("orders-svc") // The reachability probe: a metadata fetch. .connect_timeout(Duration::from_secs(5)) // Each consumer group assigning this member its partitions. .assignment_timeout(Duration::from_secs(20)) } fn app() -> impl App { service(broker("localhost:9092")) }

KafkaContext gives a handler the record's topic, partition, offset, timestamp and key, each read as a parameter through Ctx<K>. The subscription builds it once per delivery, beside the payload and the headers. A handler binds one field with Ctx<K>, where K is a key of context::keys: Key Value What it is Topic Str the topic the record was read from, which differs per record on a topic list or pattern Partition i32 the partition the record was read from Offset i64 the record's offset in its partition TimestampMillis Option<i64> the record's timestamp in milliseconds since the epoch, when it has one Key Option<Bytes> the record key, when the record has one Topic and Partition are in the prelude; the other keys are imported from context::keys. A body that reads several fields takes ctx: &mut Context<'_, KafkaContext> instead and calls ctx.context(key) per field, as the manual form does. Reading the context also hands it to the retry position, where ToSourceTopic reads the topic. The same context carries the Position and SeekHandle keys, which move the subscription through the log.

Macros Manual examples/kafka_context_fields.rs /// Each `Ctx<K>` binds one field of the record; the order's customer is its record key. #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("orders").group("audit"), reply)] async fn audit( order: &Order, Ctx(topic): Ctx<Topic>, Ctx(partition): Ctx<Partition>, Ctx(offset): Ctx<Offset>, Ctx(timestamp_millis): Ctx<TimestampMillis>, Ctx(key): Ctx<Key>, ) -> AuditRecord { let customer = key.map(|key: Bytes| String::from_utf8_lossy(&key).into_owned()); tracing::info!(order.id, %topic, partition, offset, "order audited"); AuditRecord { order_id: order.id, topic: topic.to_string(), partition, offset, timestamp_millis, customer, } } examples/manual/kafka_context_fields.rs /// The body reads each field of the record off its context by its key; the order's customer is /// its record key. struct Audit; impl Handle<Order, AuditRecord, (), KafkaContext> for Audit { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, KafkaContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<AuditRecord, HandlerOutcome>> { let topic = ctx.context(Topic).to_string(); let partition = ctx.context(Partition); let offset = ctx.context(Offset); let customer = ctx .context(Key) .map(|key| String::from_utf8_lossy(key).into_owned()); tracing::info!(order.id, %topic, partition, offset, "order audited"); ready(Ok(AuditRecord { order_id: order.id, topic, partition, offset, timestamp_millis: ctx.context(TimestampMillis), customer, })) } } fn audited() -> KafkaTopic { KafkaTopic::new("orders").group("audit") }

A batch handler's context, KafkaBatchContext, carries the subscription's seek handle; each record's own coordinates travel with the elements. A batch spans many records, so it has no single topic, partition or offset. The subscription builds the context once per batch, and it holds what every record of the batch shares: the SeekHandle key, the same key a KafkaContext carries. A batch body takes ctx: &mut Context<'_, KafkaBatchContext> and reads the handle with ctx.context(SeekHandle). A seek from a batch body takes effect once the whole batch has settled, so the next batch opens at the new position. A per-record key such as Partition or Offset is a compile error in a batch body, because the batch context does not carry it. A batch registration has no per-record topic for ToSourceTopic either, so it names a fixed retry topic.

Macros Manual examples/kafka_context_batch.rs /// The batch settles first; the seek then opens the next batch at the offset a job named, so /// the run from there is processed again. #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("jobs").group("jobs-svc").commit(Commit::Tracked))] async fn drain( jobs: &[Job], ctx: &mut Context<'_, KafkaBatchContext>, State(redos): State<Arc<Redos>>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(jobs = jobs.len(), "draining jobs"); let target = jobs .iter() .filter(|job| redos.first_time(job)) .find_map(|job| job.redo_from); if let Some((partition, offset)) = target && ctx .context(SeekHandle) .seek(KafkaPosition::offset(partition, offset)) .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_context_batch.rs /// The batch settles first; the seek then opens the next batch at the offset a job named, so /// the run from there is processed again. struct Drain; impl Handle<[Job], (), (), KafkaBatchContext, AppState> for Drain { async fn handle( &self, jobs: &[Job], _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, KafkaBatchContext, AppState>, ) -> Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(jobs = jobs.len(), "draining jobs"); let redos = &ctx.state().redos; let target = jobs .iter() .filter(|job| redos.first_time(job)) .find_map(|job| job.redo_from); if let Some((partition, offset)) = target && ctx .context(SeekHandle) .seek(KafkaPosition::offset(partition, offset)) .await .is_err() { return Err(jobs.iter().map(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()).collect()); } Ok(()) } } fn jobs() -> KafkaTopic { KafkaTopic::new("jobs") .group("jobs-svc") .commit(Commit::Tracked) }

KafkaPosition names a place in the log: either end, an offset, an offset of one topic, or a timestamp. Kafka keeps its log, so a subscription can be moved through it, at startup with start_at or from a handler with a seek. KafkaPosition::earliest() is the oldest record each partition retains, and KafkaPosition::latest() is the end of each partition's log. KafkaPosition::timestamp(millis) is, on each partition, the first record stamped at or after that time in epoch milliseconds; a partition with no such record resumes at its end. These three apply to every partition the subscription reads. KafkaPosition::offset(partition, offset) is one partition at an absolute offset, on every topic the subscription reads. KafkaPosition::topic_offset(topic, partition, offset) names the topic too, which a subscription over several topics needs. A delivery's own coordinates are a position as well: Ctx<Position> binds them, and a seek there replays that record. A position on a partition or a topic the subscription does not read is refused with an error.

A new reporting group starts from the first reading stamped at or after the time its configuration names. Macros Manual examples/kafka_positions_timestamp.rs /// Totals meter readings. #[subscriber("metering.readings")] async fn total(reading: &Reading) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(reading.id, "totalled"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The service, reading from the first record stamped at or after `since` (epoch milliseconds). fn app(servers: &str, group: &str, since: i64) -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new([servers]).default_group(group); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("metering", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(total.start_at(KafkaPosition::timestamp(since))); }) } examples/manual/kafka_positions_timestamp.rs /// Totals meter readings. struct Total; impl Handle<Reading> for Total { fn handle( &self, reading: &Reading, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(reading.id, "totalled"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// The service, reading from the first record stamped at or after `since` (epoch milliseconds). fn app(servers: &str, group: &str, since: i64) -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new([servers]).default_group(group); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("metering", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber("metering.readings", Total) .start_at(KafkaPosition::timestamp(since)) .build(), ); }) }

A handler moves its running subscription through the SeekHandle key; the seek is local and a rebalance discards it. Ctx<SeekHandle> binds a KafkaSeeker for the subscription the delivery came from. Its seek(position) takes a KafkaPosition, and the next delivery comes from there. Ctx<Partition> and Ctx<Position> give the delivery's own coordinates to aim with. A seek moves this consumer and no other member of the group. It commits nothing, and the next rebalance discards it: whoever gets the partitions resumes from the group's committed offsets. Under Commit::Tracked a seek clears the tracked position of every partition it moves, so a later commit never passes records the seek replayed and nobody handled. A seek after the service shut down returns an error. A batch handler reaches the same key through its KafkaBatchContext, and the move applies once the batch has settled. A position that has to survive a restart belongs in start_at instead.

A job that carries resume_at moves its partition past a run of jobs known to fail. Macros Manual examples/kafka_seek.rs /// Skips a run of jobs known to fail: the partition jumps to `resume_at`. #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("jobs").group("jobs-svc").commit(Commit::Tracked))] async fn work( job: &Job, Ctx(partition): Ctx<Partition>, Ctx(seeker): Ctx<SeekHandle>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(job.id, "worked"); let Some(resume_at) = job.resume_at else { return HandlerOutcome::ack(); }; match seeker .seek(KafkaPosition::offset(partition, resume_at)) .await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } examples/manual/kafka_seek.rs /// Skips a run of jobs known to fail: the partition jumps to `resume_at`. struct Work; impl Handle<Job, (), (), KafkaContext> for Work { async fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, KafkaContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { tracing::info!(job.id, "worked"); let Some(resume_at) = job.resume_at else { return Ok(()); }; let position = KafkaPosition::offset(ctx.context(Partition), resume_at); ctx.context(SeekHandle) .seek(position) .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("jobs", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let jobs = KafkaTopic::new("jobs") .group("jobs-svc") .commit(Commit::Tracked); b.include(subscriber("jobs", Work).build().map_source(|_| jobs)); }) }

start_at opens a subscription at a position on every startup, whatever the group committed. It is a clause of the attribute, start_at(KafkaPosition::earliest()), or .start_at(position) among the mount-site settings. The position lands on the partitions the subscription opened with, ahead of their first record. A subscription that opened with no partitions takes the position on the first assignment its group hands over. Under Assignment::CooperativeSticky that first assignment may be part of the group's share, and partitions that arrive in a later increment start from the committed offset. A position that names none of the partitions the subscription opened with stops the service at startup. It suits a read model rebuilt from the retained log on each boot. A group's start offset is different: it applies only where the group has committed nothing.

The audit projection is rebuilt from the oldest retained entry on every startup, although its group committed everything it read before. Macros Manual examples/kafka_seek.rs /// Rebuilds the audit projection from the oldest retained entry on every startup. #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("ledger.audit").commit(Commit::Tracked), start_at(KafkaPosition::earliest()) )] async fn replay(entry: &AuditEntry) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(entry.id, "projected"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_seek.rs /// Projects every audit entry it reads. struct Replay; impl Handle<AuditEntry> for Replay { fn handle( &self, entry: &AuditEntry, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(entry.id, "projected"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app(servers: &str, group: &str) -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new([servers]).default_group(group); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let audit = KafkaTopic::new("ledger.audit").commit(Commit::Tracked); // The projection is rebuilt from the oldest retained entry on every startup. b.include( subscriber("ledger.audit", Replay) .build() .map_source(|_| audit) .start_at(KafkaPosition::earliest()), ); }) }

A prost message rides the byte lanes as itself, and decode_confluent steps over the Confluent envelope with no registry. The protobuf feature adds it, with the protobuf module. A generated message is not a serde type, so it carries its own bytes: an incoming type derives Deserialized and names #[wire(decode = decode_confluent)], an outgoing one derives Serialized and names #[wire(encode = prost::Message::encode)]. The handler then takes and returns generated messages, and its signature says nothing about the wire. A registry-backed producer writes the Confluent envelope in front of the message: a zero byte, the four-byte schema id, and the index path of the message within its schema. decode_confluent parses all three and reads the rest into the reader's own type. No lookup is needed, because Protobuf fields are addressed by tag: an unknown field is kept as unknown, and a missing one takes its default. A payload with no envelope is read as a bare message, so a topic where only some producers frame still decodes. What the reader does not check is which schema version a delivery claims. Writing the envelope needs the schema id of the destination's subject, which a value cannot look up. The publish side adds it where the destination is known: framed at a mount site, or ProtobufFrame for the whole app. A publish without either sends the bare message. A subject is registered from .proto text through SchemaRegistry::register with SchemaType::Protobuf. The registry paths compile that text with the well-known types available, so a schema imports from them and from nothing else.

The generated types, with their lanes. examples/kafka_protobuf_plain.rs // What `prost-build` emits, plus the lane derives: the order decodes past the envelope, and the // confirmation encodes itself through `prost`. #[derive(Clone, PartialEq, prost::Message, Deserialized)] #[wire(decode = decode_confluent)] struct Order { #[prost(int64, tag = "1")] id: i64, #[prost(string, tag = "2")] item: String, } #[derive(Clone, PartialEq, prost::Message, Serialized, Outgoing)] #[wire(encode = prost::Message::encode)] #[outgoing(name = "confirmations")] struct Confirmation { #[prost(int64, tag = "1")] id: i64, #[prost(bool, tag = "2")] accepted: bool, } The handler reads a framed or a bare order and returns the confirmation, which leaves as a bare message. Macros Manual examples/kafka_protobuf_plain.rs /// Confirms an order that names an item. #[subscriber("orders", reply)] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { tracing::info!(order = order.id, item = %order.item, "confirming"); Confirmation { id: order.id, accepted: !order.item.is_empty(), } } examples/manual/kafka_protobuf_plain.rs /// Confirms an order that names an item. struct Confirm; // Both positions are generated messages that carry their own bytes, so neither names a codec. impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order = order.id, item = %order.item, "confirming"); ready(Ok(Confirmation { id: order.id, accepted: !order.item.is_empty(), })) } } Macros Manual examples/kafka_protobuf_plain.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("orders-svc"), |b| { b.include(confirm); }, ) } examples/manual/kafka_protobuf_plain.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("orders-svc"), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Confirm).reply().build()); }, ) }

KafkaPublish::framed puts the Confluent envelope on every message its policy publishes, with the destination subject's schema id. It returns a KafkaFramedPublish, a policy like any other, so it goes where a policy goes: .out_reply(..) or an Out slot. Its live form is a KafkaFramedPublisher. The subject comes from the destination topic, {topic}-value by default; subject_strategy and subject choose another. The index path names the schema's first message, which Confluent writes as one zero byte. message pins another message of the schema by its full name, for a topic whose type is not declared first. KafkaFramedPublish::over wraps a configured KafkaPublish instead of the default one. The subject is resolved on the first publish to each destination and cached. That is the first moment the destination is known: it comes from the reply clause or the slot publish, not from the policy. So a subject the registry does not hold, or one holding another format, fails that publish with the subject and the format, and the handler's failure policy settles the delivery. A payload that already carries an envelope is left as it is, so the policy and ProtobufFrame together frame a message once.

The receipt declares no destination, so the mount site's reply("order-receipts") names it, and the policy frames it with the id of order-receipts-value. Macros Manual examples/kafka_protobuf_framed.rs // The receipt names no destination, so the mount site's `reply(..)` does. #[derive(Clone, PartialEq, prost::Message, Serialized, Outgoing)] #[wire(encode = prost::Message::encode)] struct Receipt { #[prost(int64, tag = "1")] order_id: i64, #[prost(bool, tag = "2")] accepted: bool, } #[subscriber("orders", reply("order-receipts"))] async fn receipt(order: &Order) -> Receipt { Receipt { order_id: order.id, accepted: !order.item.is_empty(), } } examples/manual/kafka_protobuf_framed.rs // The receipt names no destination, so the mount site's `reply(..)` does. #[derive(Clone, PartialEq, prost::Message, Serialized, Outgoing)] #[wire(encode = prost::Message::encode)] struct Receipt { #[prost(int64, tag = "1")] order_id: i64, #[prost(bool, tag = "2")] accepted: bool, } struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Receipt> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Receipt { order_id: order.id, accepted: !order.item.is_empty(), })) } } Macros Manual examples/kafka_protobuf_framed.rs fn app(registry: &SchemaRegistry) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("orders-svc"), |b| { // The subject is the destination topic's, `order-receipts-value`, resolved on the // first reply and cached. b.include(receipt).out_reply(Publish::framed(registry)); }, ) } examples/manual/kafka_protobuf_framed.rs fn app(registry: &SchemaRegistry) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("orders-svc"), |b| { let orders = subscriber("orders", Confirm).reply().to("order-receipts"); // The subject is the destination topic's, `order-receipts-value`, resolved on the // first reply and cached. b.include(orders.build()) .out_reply(Publish::framed(registry)); }, ) }

ProtobufFrame, added with publish_layer, frames every Protobuf publish of the app that leaves through a slot. ProtobufFrame::new takes the registry, and the app adds the layer once, so no mount site names the framing. A publish is framed when its destination's subject holds a Protobuf schema. Every other publish passes as it is: a topic with no subject, and a subject holding Avro or JSON. So one app carries Protobuf, Avro and JSON topics with the layer installed. A payload that already carries an envelope also passes, so a message is never framed twice. subject_strategy, subject and message choose the subject and the message as they do on framed. The layer sees what leaves through an Out slot and through a publisher the runtime pairs. A reply returned from a reply(..) handler goes straight to its paired publisher, so it is framed by naming framed at its mount site. The layer is an alternative to the transcode's SchemaFrame: this one expects the payload to be the Protobuf datum already, that one expects JSON.

Every order writes an audit record through a slot, and the layer frames it with the id of order-audit-value. Macros Manual examples/kafka_protobuf_frame.rs #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Audit)] struct Journal; /// Records every order in the audit journal; the app's layer frames the record. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn audit(order: &Order, Out(journal): Out<impl Publisher, Journal>) -> HandlerOutcome { let record = Audit { order_id: order.id }; if journal.message(&record).publish().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_protobuf_frame.rs struct Journal; impl OutSlot for Journal { const NAME: &'static str = "Journal"; type Destination = Reads; } impl PublishedThrough<Journal> for Audit {} /// Records every order in the audit journal; the app's layer frames the record. struct AuditOrder; impl<J> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(J,)>> for AuditOrder where J: OutEntry<Journal, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(J,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let record = Audit { order_id: order.id }; if outs.get(Journal).message(&record).publish().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } Macros Manual examples/kafka_protobuf_frame.rs fn app(registry: &SchemaRegistry) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Frames every publish whose destination subject holds a Protobuf schema. .publish_layer(ProtobufFrame::new(registry.clone())) .with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("orders-svc"), |b| { b.include(audit).out(Journal, Publish::default()).build(); }, ) } examples/manual/kafka_protobuf_frame.rs fn app(registry: &SchemaRegistry) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Frames every publish whose destination subject holds a Protobuf schema. .publish_layer(ProtobufFrame::new(registry.clone())) .with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("orders-svc"), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", AuditOrder).build()) .out(Journal, Publish::default()) .build(); }, ) }

On a broker with schema_registry, framed Protobuf arrives as JSON and leaves framed, with no generated code in the service. Every subscription of that broker reads a delivery's schema id, fetches the schema and compiles its .proto source into a descriptor. It decodes the datum into a dynamic message and hands the handler JSON, so the handler is a plain serde one on the default codec. On the way out, the SchemaFrame publish layer turns the JSON into the subject's Protobuf message and frames it. Field names in the serde types match the .proto messages. The message written is the schema's first; SchemaFrame::message pins another. This path is for a service that does not carry generated types. It costs a JSON hop and a dynamic message per delivery, and nothing decodes while the registry is unreachable. A service with generated types reads them on the byte lanes with decode_confluent instead. The two do not mix on one broker: a broker with schema_registry transcodes every subscription, so a generated type there would be handed JSON.

The .proto source of the reply's subject and the serde types. examples/kafka_protobuf_transcode.rs /// What the `order-confirmations-value` subject holds: the registry keeps Protobuf as `.proto` /// source. const CONFIRMATION_PROTO: &str = r#" syntax = "proto3"; package shop; message Confirmation { int64 id = 1; bool accepted = 2; } "#; // Plain serde structs whose field names match the `.proto` messages. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Order { id: i64, item: String, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "order-confirmations")] struct Confirmation { id: i64, accepted: bool, } The handler is an ordinary JSON one. Macros Manual examples/kafka_protobuf_transcode.rs /// An ordinary handler on the default JSON codec. #[subscriber("orders", reply)] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { Confirmation { id: order.id, accepted: !order.item.is_empty(), } } examples/manual/kafka_protobuf_transcode.rs /// An ordinary handler on the default JSON codec. struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Confirmation { id: order.id, accepted: !order.item.is_empty(), })) } } The broker transcodes the deliveries, the layer frames the replies, and startup registers the reply's subject. Macros Manual examples/kafka_protobuf_transcode.rs fn app(registry: &SchemaRegistry) -> impl App { // Every subscription of this broker turns a framed delivery into JSON. let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]) .default_group("orders-svc") .schema_registry(registry.clone()); let subjects = registry.clone(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Writes framed Protobuf where the destination's subject holds a Protobuf schema. .publish_layer(SchemaFrame::new(registry.clone())) .on_startup(async move |()| { subjects .register( "order-confirmations-value", SchemaType::Protobuf, CONFIRMATION_PROTO, ) .await?; Ok::<_, KafkaError>(()) }) .with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(confirm); }) } examples/manual/kafka_protobuf_transcode.rs fn app(registry: &SchemaRegistry) -> impl App { // Every subscription of this broker turns a framed delivery into JSON. let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]) .default_group("orders-svc") .schema_registry(registry.clone()); let subjects = registry.clone(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Writes framed Protobuf where the destination's subject holds a Protobuf schema. .publish_layer(SchemaFrame::new(registry.clone())) .on_startup(async move |()| { subjects .register( "order-confirmations-value", SchemaType::Protobuf, CONFIRMATION_PROTO, ) .await?; Ok::<_, KafkaError>(()) }) .with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Confirm).reply().build()); }) }

KafkaPublish, Publish in the prelude, is the plain publish policy; every publish waits for the cluster's delivery report. A mount site names it wherever a registration publishes: .out_reply(Publish::default()) for a reply, .out(Slot, Publish::default()) for a slot, .out_retry(Publish::default()) for retry copies. The policy holds no connection; the runtime pairs it with the connected broker at startup into a KafkaPublisher. A registration that names no policy for its reply publishes through this one. A publish returns once the cluster has acknowledged the record, as the producer's durability settings define it, or with the error it reported. librdkafka queues records locally and sends them in batches; a full queue makes a publish wait for room, which slows the handler to the pace of the cluster. queue_timeout bounds that wait: past it the publish fails with a queue-full error. A reply goes to one topic and does not wait for an answer from the reader. A synchronous exchange is a reply topic of the service's own plus a correlation header the requester sets and the responder copies to its reply. Per record, a publish carries a key or a partition; RoundRobin spreads replies over the partitions.

Macros Manual examples/kafka_publishing_publish.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]), |b| { // A full local queue fails the reply after five seconds instead of holding the // handler until librdkafka has room again. b.include(confirm) .out_reply(Publish::default().queue_timeout(Duration::from_secs(5))); }, ) } examples/manual/kafka_publishing_publish.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]), |b| { let confirm = subscriber("orders", Confirm).map_source(|_| orders()); // A full local queue fails the reply after five seconds instead of holding the // handler until librdkafka has room again. b.include(confirm.reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish::default().queue_timeout(Duration::from_secs(5))); }, ) }

Durability is the producer's acks; an idempotent producer with Commit::Tracked gives at-least-once from input to output. producer_config sets a librdkafka producer property on the broker, for every publisher of the service. acks says which replicas confirm a record before a publish returns: all waits for every in-sync replica. enable.idempotence makes the producer number its sends, so the cluster writes a record once even when the producer sends it again. librdkafka checks the values when the broker connects, so a wrong value stops the service at startup. A handler that replies settles its input after the reply's publish returned. Under Commit::Tracked the input's offset is committed only then, so a crash before it brings the input back and the reply is sent again. A reader of the output can therefore see a reply twice; exactly once takes a transactional pipeline.

Macros Manual examples/kafka_publishing_durability.rs /// The input's offset is committed once the receipt is acknowledged by every in-sync replica, /// so a crash in between brings the payment back instead of losing the receipt. #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("payments").group("receipts-svc").commit(Commit::Tracked), reply)] async fn issue_receipt(payment: &Payment) -> Receipt { Receipt { payment_id: payment.id, } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { // Every in-sync replica confirms a record, and a retried send is written once. let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]) .producer_config("acks", "all") .producer_config("enable.idempotence", "true"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("receipts", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(issue_receipt).out_reply(Publish::default()); }) } examples/manual/kafka_publishing_durability.rs /// The input's offset is committed once the receipt is acknowledged by every in-sync replica, /// so a crash in between brings the payment back instead of losing the receipt. struct IssueReceipt; impl Handle<Payment, Receipt> for IssueReceipt { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Receipt { payment_id: payment.id, })) } } fn payments() -> KafkaTopic { KafkaTopic::new("payments") .group("receipts-svc") .commit(Commit::Tracked) } fn app() -> impl App { // Every in-sync replica confirms a record, and a retried send is written once. let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]) .producer_config("acks", "all") .producer_config("enable.idempotence", "true"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("receipts", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let issue = subscriber("payments", IssueReceipt).map_source(|_| payments()); b.include(issue.reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish::default()); }) }

The partition-key header, PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, becomes the record's native key, so records sharing a key land on one partition, in order. The header is named kafka-partition-key. On publish its value becomes the Kafka record key and does not travel as a header of its own. Kafka's partitioner hashes the key, so every record of one key goes to one partition, and a consumer reads them in the order they were written. A message type declares the header in its typed header contract, #[outgoing(headers = ..)], with a field renamed to kafka-partition-key; a HeaderMap with that entry works the same. On consume the header holds the record key again, and a handler reads the key as raw bytes through the Key context key. workers(n, by_key) with LaneKey::RecordKey keeps the same order inside one consumer: records of one key run on one lane. A partition step places a record ahead of its key.

The partition step pins one record to a partition, ahead of its key and the partitioner. It is a per-record setting of Kafka's publisher, KafkaOptions, written by a step of the publish builder. A handler reaches the step through a slot bounded on those options: Out<impl Publisher<Options = KafkaOptions>, Slot>, with this crate's prelude imported. The bound keeps the step off a publisher of another broker. The record goes to exactly that partition; its key still travels with it. A partition the topic does not have fails the publish, and the handler decides what follows. A test reads the setting back from the slot with tb.out::<Slot>().with_options(..). The in-process cluster gives every topic one partition, so a pin to partition 0 lands and a pin to any other is refused, as a cluster refuses a partition its topic lacks.

RoundRobin spreads replies over a fixed partition count, placing only records with no key and no partition. librdkafka places a keyless record by its partitioner, which may keep a whole batch on one partition. When every message takes about the same long time to process, that leaves one consumer busy and its peers idle. RoundRobin::partitions(n) pins each record to the next partition of the cycle 0, 1, ..., n - 1, one record each. It is a transform of the publish position, written after the policy: .out_reply(Publish::default()).transform(RoundRobin::partitions(n)). It writes the same setting as the partition step, so it mounts over Kafka's publisher only. A record that carries a key or already names a partition keeps its placement. The count is fixed at the mount site and matches the destination topic: a smaller one leaves the last partitions empty, a larger one makes publishes fail.

SchemaRegistry is the Confluent Schema Registry client: it sends nothing until the first lookup, and its clones share one cache. SchemaRegistry::new records the base URL, so the app starts with no registry reachable. basic_auth and bearer_token set the credentials of every request, and HTTPS goes through rustls. request_timeout bounds each request, ten seconds by default, so a registry that accepts the connection and goes silent fails the lookup with KafkaError::SchemaRegistryTimeout. The client is configured before it is handed out, because clones keep the settings they were made from. Every clone reads and writes one cache, so a schema or a subject is fetched once per process. schema_by_id answers from the cache or asks the registry once; cached_schema and cached_subject read the cache alone. A RegisteredSchema carries the id, the SchemaType (Avro, Protobuf or JSON) and the definition text. A registry-backed payload carries the Confluent envelope: a zero byte, the schema id, then the datum. A broker meets it in one of two ways. The codecs, AvroCodec and SchemaFramed, hold the format where a serializer belongs and take their schemas through a SchemaPrefetch. The transcode converts at the broker's edges and leaves the handlers on plain JSON. The example holds the client as application state, and a handler asks it which schema a record was written with.

SchemaCachePolicy bounds the id entries and ages the subject entries, since an id never changes and a subject's latest version moves. The registry assigns an id per distinct schema, so an entry keyed by id is never stale; it takes a bound and no expiry. A subject's latest version moves whenever someone registers one, so its entry takes an expiry and no bound. Cached holds up to capacity ids, drops the oldest past it, and trusts a subject's version for subject_ttl. The default keeps 1000 ids and never looks a subject up again, as Confluent's own clients do. Disabled remembers nothing: the transcode works under it, and the synchronous codecs, which read the cache and cannot await a miss, do not. subject_ttl governs the async lookups: warm and the publish side of the transcode. A codec resolves its subject once, at connect, and keeps it. Ids are numbered per schema context, so one client stays inside one context; an app that reaches across contexts uses a client per context. SchemaRegistry::cache_policy sets the policy of the default cache, MemorySchemaCache. with_cache puts a SchemaCache of your own in its place. That trait is synchronous, because a codec reads it while it encodes or decodes; fetching belongs to the RegistryClient.

parse_envelope and encode_envelope read and write the Confluent wire format: a zero byte, the schema id, the datum. The schema id takes four bytes, big-endian. parse_envelope splits a payload into the id and a view of the datum, with no copy. It returns None for a payload that does not open with the zero byte or is shorter than five bytes, which reads as "not framed". encode_envelope writes the five bytes and the datum into a new buffer. Neither function reaches a registry. A handler that works on the framed bytes takes them through the byte lanes: a #[derive(Deserialized)] view of the delivery in, a #[derive(Serialized)] buffer out. No codec runs on either side, so the bytes travel as they are. The example moves records between two registries and rewrites the id each record names.

schema_registry on the broker and the SchemaFrame layer convert framed payloads to and from plain JSON at the broker's edges. The handler and its models stay on the default JSON codec and never see the envelope. On the way in, every subscription of the broker reads the envelope of a framed delivery, resolves the schema its id names and hands the handler a plain JSON document. A payload with no envelope passes through untouched. A lookup that fails leaves the delivery as it arrived, with a warning, and the handler's decode settles it. On the way out, the layer, added once with RustStream::publish_layer, resolves the subject of each publish's destination topic and frames the payload in that subject's format: a JSON subject keeps the document under the envelope, and an Avro or Protobuf subject is converted to its own format. The subject is {topic}-value unless SubjectStrategy or a pin names another. The layer resolves a subject on its first publish to the topic and remembers the answer. A topic whose subject the registry does not hold publishes plain JSON, so registry-backed and plain topics share one app. A registry that cannot be reached, or a payload that does not fit the schema, fails the publish, and the publishing handler asks for a redelivery. The registry comes to the app as one SchemaRegistry value; the broker and the layer share it, and with it one cache. A producer owns its subjects, so the example registers the reply's subject at startup with register_json. The transcode takes a hop through JSON per message. The codecs (SchemaFramed, AvroCodec) are the other path, and a broker uses one of the two.

MissingSubject decides what a codec does when the registry no longer holds its subject: refuse, register the type's schema, or publish unframed. The policy is set on the prefetch with on_missing_subject before codecs are built from it, and it runs when the broker connects. Refuse, the default, stops the app with an error that names the subject: a registry is a shared contract, and creating a subject in it belongs to whoever owns the topic. AutoRegister registers the schema the type carries under the subject and logs a warning; it suits a producer that owns its subjects. PublishUnframed writes the bare datum and logs a warning, for a topic that must outlive its registry; a registry-backed consumer cannot read those records. The two deletions of a subject differ. A soft delete hides the subject while its ids still resolve, so consumers keep reading and only the producer meets the policy. A permanent delete removes the ids too, and a record that names one of them no longer decodes anywhere. Registering the schema again afterwards mints a new id. The transcode reads a missing subject as a plain topic and publishes JSON there. Naming a codec declares its topic registry-backed, so the policy belongs to the codecs.

register, register_json and register_avro put a schema under a subject; warm resolves an existing subject and registers nothing. Registering is an explicit step of the producer that owns the subject, usually in on_startup. The registry keeps the id of a schema it already holds, so registering the same schema again changes nothing. A schema that the subject's compatibility level refuses fails the call, and the error carries the registry's account of what differs. Each call caches the subject, so the SchemaFrame layer finds it without a request. register_json::<T> registers the JSON Schema that JsonSchema (schemars, re-exported) derives for T. register_avro::<T> registers the Avro schema that AvroSchema derives, in full: field defaults, aliases and docs stay, because a later reader resolves an older writer's datum with them. register takes a SchemaType and the definition text, which is how a Protobuf subject is registered from its .proto source. The registry paths of this crate read Protobuf schemas whose imports come from the well-known types. warm resolves a subject's latest version and caches it, and fails when the registry has no such subject. It is the startup check of a subject that another team owns. lookup_id returns the id a subject already gave one exact schema, and is_compatible asks whether the subject would accept a schema; neither registers anything. A codec registers in its own sense: AvroCodec::register and SchemaFramed::register record the subject a type publishes under, and the SchemaPrefetch resolves those subjects when the broker connects. The registry itself is named twice in such an app, building the prefetch and attaching it, and never at a mount site.

RegistryClient is the transport the registry speaks through; HttpRegistryClient is the default, and with_client supplies another. SchemaRegistry is a facade over two parts: a RegistryClient that asks the registry, and a SchemaCache that remembers the answers. The codecs, the prefetch and the transcode are written against the facade, so a client of your own reaches all of them. It suits a different HTTP stack, a published client crate, a binding to a client in another language, or schemas shipped with the service. A client answers four questions, each as a boxed future: a schema by id, a subject's latest version, registering a schema, and the id of a schema a subject already holds. latest answers None for a subject the registry does not hold, which the transcode reads as a plain topic. is_compatible has a default that answers None, "cannot tell", and the prefetch then skips its compatibility check. The client is shared as Arc<dyn RegistryClient>, so each round trip costs one virtual call and one allocation beside the network, and only a lookup the cache does not answer makes one. basic_auth, bearer_token and request_timeout configure the shipped HTTP client, and a supplied client carries its own credentials and deadlines. Errors are KafkaError::SchemaRegistry, with a message that names what was asked.

SchemaFramed wraps a codec such as JsonCodec in the Confluent envelope, so a registry-backed JSON topic is a codec choice. A JSON document reads without its schema, so the envelope separates from the format: the inner codec writes and reads the document, and SchemaFramed puts the envelope on and takes it off. Decoding strips the envelope and looks nothing up. Encoding frames with the id of the subject that register::<T>(subject) records for T, found by the name serde gives the value's type. The JSON Schema of T is captured with it, for MissingSubject::AutoRegister. The wrapper frames and does not validate: the registry enforces compatibility between versions, and a service that validates each message passes an inner codec that does. SchemaFramed::new takes the SchemaPrefetch that the broker carries, which resolves the registered subjects at connect. The codec named with with_broker_codec decodes the deliveries of its scope, and a reply names it at its own position with .out_reply(policy).codec(codec). An Avro datum cannot be read without its writer schema, so Avro has a codec of its own, AvroCodec.

SchemaPrefetch resolves every registered subject at connect, which keeps the codecs' encode and decode free of I/O. A codec is synchronous, and a registry lookup is not. The prefetch is the async half: every codec built from it, AvroCodec::registry or SchemaFramed::new, records its registered subjects on it. KafkaBroker::schema_prefetch attaches it, and the broker's connect resolves each subject before the app takes a delivery. On the consume path the prefetch resolves the writer schema that an arriving envelope names before the codec decodes the delivery, and leaves the payload as it arrived. A lookup that fails there is logged, and the decode that follows settles the delivery by the subscription's failure policy. The registry appears twice in an app: once building the prefetch, once attaching it. A mount site never names it. Every codec comes from the one prefetch, and what varies per mount is the subject. A Router inside a broker scope overrides the scope's codec for the handlers it carries, by the usual codec cascade. check_compatibility is on by default. At connect each registered type's schema is checked the way registering it would be, against the versions the subject's compatibility level names: the latest one, or every version under a _TRANSITIVE level. A model that has drifted from its subject stops the app, and the error carries the registry's own account of the difference. check_compatibility(false) turns the check off, for a registry whose level is NONE. A subject the registry does not hold is settled by MissingSubject. The prefetch and the transcode are alternatives on one broker: the prefetch reads the envelope, and the transcode replaces it with JSON.

SubjectStrategy names a subject from the topic, the record name or both, and SchemaFrame::subject pins the subject of one topic. The strategies are Confluent's three. TopicName, the default, is {topic}-value: one value schema per topic. RecordName is the record's fully qualified name: one subject per record type, shared by every topic that carries it. TopicRecordName is {topic}-{record}: several record types on one topic, each with its own subject. subject(topic, record) builds the name. The SchemaFrame layer derives a topic's subject with its strategy, TopicName unless subject_strategy names another. The publish path knows the topic and not the record name, so a topic under a record strategy gets its subject pinned with subject(topic, subject), which overrides the strategy for that topic. The example pins the subject that RecordName gives the record. The Protobuf publish policy and its layer take the same three settings.

Another registry stack does the schema work and the byte lanes carry its framed bytes, so no type crosses between the two. A service that already uses a registry crate, such as schema_registry_converter, keeps it. The handler takes the delivery as a #[derive(Deserialized)] view of its bytes and hands them to the converter, which resolves the schema the envelope names through its own client and cache. The reply is the framed buffer the converter returns, in a #[derive(Serialized)] type, and the lane publishes it as it is. No codec runs on either side. Such a crate pins its own apache-avro and prost, and those versions may differ from this crate's. On this path only bytes pass between the two, so the versions never meet. The converter is application state, built in on_startup and read with State. The broker carries neither schema_registry nor schema_prefetch: the schemas are the converter's business. The same shape fits any client that produces bytes, a binding to a client in another language included.

Commit decides what an ack or a nack does on Kafka, which settles a consumer group by committed position, not per message. A consumer group stores one offset per partition: the position its next member starts reading at. A handler settles one delivery at a time, so the subscription has to turn those outcomes into that one position. The descriptor chooses how with .commit(..): KafkaTopic, KafkaTopics and KafkaPartitions all take it. Commit::Auto is the default: librdkafka stores the position as a record is handed over and commits it on a timer. Commit::Tracked moves the position only past deliveries the handlers have settled, so a crash brings back what was not finished. Commit::Transactional hands the offsets to an exactly-once pipeline, which commits them in the producer's transaction. Under Tracked an ack and a drop both settle the offset, and nothing comes back. A retry hands the delivery back to its subscription instead.

Commit::Auto is librdkafka's timer commit: an ack is advisory, and a retry is not delivered again. It is the default of every descriptor, and librdkafka's own default. librdkafka stores a record's position as it hands the record to the subscription, and commits the stored position every auto.commit.interval.ms. The handler's outcome changes nothing about that position: an ack and a drop are advisory. A retry reports itself unsupported, and the delivery does not come back on the subscription or on the group's next member. A crash loses the processed records whose position was not committed yet, and skips the stored records the handler had not finished. This suits a consumer that can lose a few records, such as a dashboard or a cache. A consumer that must process every record takes Commit::Tracked.

dead_letter(topic) names the topic a delivery that reached its cap is republished to, payload and headers as they arrived. It follows max_attempts(n) at the mount site. When a retry would make the delivery the n-th one, the runtime settles it and publishes it to the dead-letter topic instead. The record keeps its payload, its headers and its record key. RETRY_COUNT_HEADER on it says how many times it was delivered. A cap without a dead-letter topic rejects the spent delivery, which settles its offset, and a warning names the subscription. The dead-letter topic is the service's own infrastructure, an ordinary topic: a subscription of the same service, or of another one, reads it.

retry_after(delay) asks for a later delivery: the runtime republishes a copy to the subscription with its delivery count in a header. Kafka holds no record back and counts no deliveries, so the runtime does both. It settles the delivery, waits out the delay and publishes a copy of the record, payload and headers, to the topic the subscription reads. The copy carries RETRY_COUNT_HEADER incremented, and the handler reads it like any other header. The copy waits in the service's memory, so it is at-most-once over the delay: a process that exits before the timer fires loses it. max_attempts(n) caps the deliveries of one record at the mount site, the first one included. Under a cap every retry, an immediate one too, travels as such a copy, because the count lives in the header. The delivery that reaches the cap goes to the dead-letter topic. The copies leave through the Retry slot, which out_retry replaces. A subscription over several topics names where its copies go, as ToSourceTopic shows.

ToSourceTopic sends each retry copy back to the topic its delivery arrived on, for subscriptions over several topics. A KafkaTopic subscription reads one topic, and its retry copies go there. A KafkaTopics list or pattern and a KafkaPartitions reader have no single topic, so the mount site names one. ToSourceTopic is a transform of the Retry slot: .out_retry(Publish::default()).transform(ToSourceTopic). It reads each delivery's topic from its Kafka context, so a copy of an orders-us record goes back to orders-us. The context reaches the slot when the handler reads it: a Ctx<Topic> parameter, or a manual body typed over KafkaContext. A batch handler carries no per-record topic, so a batch registration names a fixed topic instead. .out_retry(Publish::default()).to(topic) sends every copy to that one topic; a pattern that matches it reads the copies back. A registration over several topics that names neither does not start.

Commit::Tracked commits below the lowest unsettled delivery, so a retry comes back and nothing is committed past it. The subscription stores a position only when a handler settles a delivery. The stored position is the offset just below the lowest delivery still in flight, so handlers that finish out of order, on several workers, never commit past an unfinished one. librdkafka's timer commits the stored position in the background and once more when the consumer closes. An ack and a drop settle the offset. A retry hands the delivery back to its subscription, which delivers it again before the records behind it. Until it is settled, the group's committed position stays below it, so a crash or a rebalance brings it to the next member. Offsets the consumer never receives, such as transaction markers and compacted records, do not hold the position back. Tracked with an idempotent producer gives at-least-once from input to output, as Durability shows.

A topic name in #[subscriber] reads that topic in the broker's default group; a descriptor carries every other setting. #[subscriber("orders")] reads the topic orders. Kafka reads a topic only through a consumer group, and a bare name names none, so the group comes from KafkaBroker::default_group. A subscription with no group, on a broker with no default group, stops the service at startup with an error that names the subscription. Two subscriptions of one name and one group are two members of that group: each record goes to one of them. Every other setting of a subscription belongs to a descriptor: KafkaTopic for one topic, KafkaTopics for several topics or a pattern, and KafkaPartitions for named partitions. A descriptor goes where the name goes, as the attribute's first argument. The manual form passes the name to subscriber(name, body), and a descriptor joins the chain through map_source. A subscription is open once its group has assigned it its partitions, so everything published after startup reaches it. Startup waits for that assignment up to KafkaBroker::assignment_timeout, 60 seconds by default.

Assignment picks the consumer group's rebalance strategy, eager or cooperative sticky. A group hands each partition of its topics to one member, and hands them out again when a member joins or leaves. The setting is librdkafka's partition.assignment.strategy, written on the descriptor with assignment. Assignment::Range and Assignment::RoundRobin are eager: every member gives up all its partitions at each rebalance, and the group stops reading until the new assignment lands. Assignment::CooperativeSticky is incremental: only the partitions that change hands move, and the rest keep flowing during the rebalance. Without the setting librdkafka uses range,roundrobin. Every member of one group must use the same family: librdkafka refuses a cooperative member in an eager group, and the error surfaces on the subscription. KafkaPartitions joins no group and has no assignment.

A cooperative sticky group reads every shipment once, whichever member holds its partition.
