}, ) }

KafkaEosPublish commits consumed offsets inside the producer's transaction, so positions move atomically with the records published. It is the consume-transform-produce shape of Kafka (KIP-447), named EosPublish in the prelude. KafkaEosPublish::new takes the pipeline id, which is also the producer's transactional id. Each source subscription names the same id in Commit::Transactional: its consumer stops committing on its own, and the pipeline commits its offsets. One pipeline serves every lane of a workers(n, by_key) pool: publishes join the open transaction concurrently, and only the commit is exclusive. The pipeline works in windows. Every commit_interval (100 ms by default) it waits until the window's deliveries have settled, adds their positions and the group's metadata to the transaction, and commits. A record becomes visible at that commit, so end-to-end latency is at least the interval. A failed publish, a failed commit or a participant that does not settle in time aborts the window. The consumers then seek back to the last committed offsets, and the whole window is delivered and published again in a fresh transaction, so the output topic never holds a duplicate. A retry() from a participant holds its window until the transaction deadline, transaction_timeout. The retry_after copy does not apply to the pipeline's replies: a delayed copy would separate the record from its offset. The window's commit runs on the runtime the broker connected on, so a handler on a dedicated thread may open a window. The transactional commit needs consumer group membership. So Commit::Transactional is a KafkaTopic or KafkaTopics mode; KafkaPartitions, which joins no group, works with Commit::Auto and Commit::Tracked. A replying handler reaches the window through EosReplies, and a handler that publishes by hand through EosPipeline.

An order is priced, and the priced order commits together with the offset of the order it answers. Macros Manual examples/kafka_eos.rs /// Prices an order; the subscription commits its offsets through the `pricing-1` pipeline. #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("raw-orders").commit(Commit::Transactional("pricing-1".into())), reply )] async fn price(order: &Order) -> PricedOrder { PricedOrder { id: order.id, cents: order.cents, tax_cents: order.cents / 5, } } examples/manual/kafka_eos.rs /// Prices an order; the subscription commits its offsets through the `pricing-1` pipeline. struct Price; impl Handle<Order, PricedOrder> for Price { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<PricedOrder, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(PricedOrder { id: order.id, cents: order.cents, tax_cents: order.cents / 5, })) } } Macros Manual examples/kafka_eos.rs fn app() -> impl App { // The policy's id is the pipeline the subscription names, and the producer's transactional id. let pipeline = EosPublish::new("pricing-1").commit_interval(Duration::from_millis(100)); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("pricing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("pricing-svc"), |b| { b.include(price).out_reply(pipeline).transform(EosReplies); }, ) } examples/manual/kafka_eos.rs fn app() -> impl App { // The policy's id is the pipeline the subscription names, and the producer's transactional id. let pipeline = EosPublish::new("pricing-1").commit_interval(Duration::from_millis(100)); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("pricing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("pricing-svc"), |b| { let orders = subscriber("raw-orders", Price) .map_source(|_| { KafkaTopic::new("raw-orders").commit(Commit::Transactional("pricing-1".into())) }) .reply(); b.include(orders.build()) .out_reply(pipeline) .transform(EosReplies); }, ) }

EosPipeline::publish sends a record into the open window by hand, with the source coordinates the Source key gives. EosPipeline is the live form of EosPublish, so a slot bound to that policy holds one. A handler reaches it through the slot's Borrow<EosPipeline> bound, Out<impl Borrow<EosPipeline>>, and the manual form names it as the slot's wired value. The delivery's coordinates are a SourceOffset, read with Ctx<Source> (context::keys::Source). publish(&source, record, options) adds the record to the window and pairs it with that offset; None keeps the producer's own partition choice. A handler publishes as many records as it needs, then acks: the settled delivery is what lets the window commit. A failed publish poisons the window, which aborts and is delivered again, so the handler answers it with retry(). The record is an OutgoingMessage the handler encodes itself. id returns the pipeline id.

A cart is split into one record per item, and every record commits with the cart's offset. Macros Manual examples/kafka_eos_pipeline.rs /// Splits a cart into one record per item, all committed with the cart's offset. #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("carts").commit(Commit::Transactional("checkout-1".into())))] async fn split( cart: &Cart, Ctx(source): Ctx<Source>, Out(window): Out<impl Borrow<EosPipeline>>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { // The slot holds the paired pipeline, and `Borrow` is the bound that reaches it. let pipeline: &EosPipeline = (**window).borrow(); for item in &cart.items { let line = CartLine { cart_id: cart.id, item: item.clone(), }; let Ok(payload) = serde_json::to_vec(&line) else { return HandlerOutcome::drop(); }; let record = OutgoingMessage::new("cart-lines", payload.as_slice()); // A failed publish aborts the window, which redelivers the cart. if pipeline.publish(&source, record, None).await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_eos_pipeline.rs /// Splits a cart into one record per item, all committed with the cart's offset. struct Split; impl<W> Handle<Cart, (), Outs<(W,)>, KafkaContext> for Split where W: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire = EosPipeline>, { async fn handle( &self, cart: &Cart, outs: &Outs<(W,)>, ctx: &mut Context<'_, KafkaContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let pipeline: &EosPipeline = outs.get(DefaultSlot); let source = ctx.context(Source); for item in &cart.items { let line = CartLine { cart_id: cart.id, item: item.clone(), }; let Ok(payload) = serde_json::to_vec(&line) else { return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); }; let record = OutgoingMessage::new("cart-lines", payload.as_slice()); // A failed publish aborts the window, which redelivers the cart. if pipeline.publish(&source, record, None).await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } } Ok(()) } } Macros Manual examples/kafka_eos_pipeline.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("checkout", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("checkout-svc"), |b| { b.include(split) .out(DefaultSlot, EosPublish::new("checkout-1")) .build(); }, ) } examples/manual/kafka_eos_pipeline.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("checkout", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("checkout-svc"), |b| { let carts = subscriber("carts", Split).map_source(|_| { KafkaTopic::new("carts").commit(Commit::Transactional("checkout-1".into())) }); b.include(carts.build()) .out(DefaultSlot, EosPublish::new("checkout-1")) .build(); }, ) }

EosReplies joins every reply to the pipeline's open window, paired with its delivery's consumed offset. It is a publish transform for the reply position, written after the policy: .out_reply(EosPublish::new(id)).transform(EosReplies). A Commit::Transactional subscription marks each delivery with its source coordinates, and the transform carries them onto the reply. The pipeline reads them, pairs the reply with that offset, and drops them before the record is produced, so they never reach the topic. The handler only returns its value: it names no publisher and no offset. Without the transform, a reply carries no coordinates and its publish fails with KafkaError::InvalidOptions, so nothing leaves outside the window. A reply from a subscription in another commit mode fails the same way. A handler that settles without a reply, a drop or an Err(outcome), publishes nothing, and its offset still commits with the window.

A payment is booked on a pool of four lanes; a payment of zero is dropped. Macros Manual examples/kafka_eos_replies.rs /// Books a payment; an empty one is dropped, and its offset still commits with the window. #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("payments").commit(Commit::Transactional("ledger-1".into())), reply, workers(4, by_key) )] async fn book(payment: &Payment) -> Result<LedgerEntry, HandlerOutcome> { if payment.cents == 0 { return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } Ok(LedgerEntry { payment_id: payment.id, cents: payment.cents, }) } examples/manual/kafka_eos_replies.rs /// Books a payment; an empty one is dropped, and its offset still commits with the window. struct Book; impl Handle<Payment, LedgerEntry> for Book { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<LedgerEntry, HandlerOutcome>> { if payment.cents == 0 { return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } ready(Ok(LedgerEntry { payment_id: payment.id, cents: payment.cents, })) } } Macros Manual examples/kafka_eos_replies.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("ledger-svc"), |b| { // The transform carries each delivery's coordinates onto its reply, where the pipeline // pairs them. b.include(book) .out_reply(EosPublish::new("ledger-1")) .transform(EosReplies); }, ) } examples/manual/kafka_eos_replies.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("ledger-svc"), |b| { let payments = subscriber("payments", Book) .map_source(|_| { KafkaTopic::new("payments").commit(Commit::Transactional("ledger-1".into())) }) .reply() .workers_by_key(nonzero!(4)); // The transform carries each delivery's coordinates onto its reply, where the pipeline // pairs them. b.include(payments.build()) .out_reply(EosPublish::new("ledger-1")) .transform(EosReplies); }, ) }

per_partition gives each source partition its own transactional publisher, so a worker pool runs independent transactions. It turns the policy into a KafkaPartitionedPublish, named PartitionedPublish in the prelude. The transactional id becomes a base: the publisher of partition 3 is fenced by "{base}-p3". A handler bounds its slot Out<impl PartitionLanes> and reads its delivery's partition through Ctx<Partition>. PartitionLanes::for_partition returns that partition's publisher, created and initialized on first use. The live value is TransactionalPartitions, and its clones share the publishers. The scope is the source partition because one producer runs one transaction at a time. Under the default LaneKey::Partition, a workers(n, by_key) pool processes each partition in order on one lane, so each lane has a transaction of its own. The set of ids follows the topic's partitions, not the worker count: changing n keeps the ids and their fencing. It does not combine with LaneKey::RecordKey, which spreads one partition over several lanes; two lanes would then meet on one producer and get KafkaError::TransactionBusy. What a lane publishes leaves through the partition's own publisher, so a test reads it on the topic, not on the slot's record.

An invoice's lines are published in the transaction of the invoice's source partition. Macros Manual examples/kafka_transactions_partitions.rs /// Bills every line of an invoice in the transaction of the invoice's source partition. #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("invoice-batches").commit(Commit::Tracked), workers(4, by_key) )] async fn bill( invoice: &Invoice, Ctx(partition): Ctx<Partition>, Out(lanes): Out<impl PartitionLanes>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let Ok(lane) = lanes.for_partition(partition).await else { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); }; if lane.begin_transaction().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } for &amount in &invoice.amounts { let entry = InvoiceLine { invoice_id: invoice.id, amount, }; if lane.message(&entry).publish().await.is_err() { lane.abort().await.ok(); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } } if lane.commit().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_transactions_partitions.rs /// Bills every line of an invoice in the transaction of the invoice's source partition. struct Bill; impl<L> Handle<Invoice, (), Outs<(L,)>, KafkaContext> for Bill where L: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: PartitionLanes>, { async fn handle( &self, invoice: &Invoice, outs: &Outs<(L,)>, ctx: &mut Context<'_, KafkaContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let partition = ctx.context(Partition); let Ok(lane) = outs.get(DefaultSlot).for_partition(partition).await else { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); }; if lane.begin_transaction().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } for &amount in &invoice.amounts { let entry = InvoiceLine { invoice_id: invoice.id, amount, }; if lane.message(&entry).publish().await.is_err() { lane.abort().await.ok(); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } } if lane.commit().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } Macros Manual examples/kafka_transactions_partitions.rs fn app(servers: &str) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new([servers]).default_group("billing-svc"), |b| { // One transactional id per source partition: "billing-svc-1-p0", "billing-svc-1-p1". let lanes = Publish::default() .transactional_id("billing-svc-1") .per_partition(); b.include(bill).out(DefaultSlot, lanes).build(); }, ) } examples/manual/kafka_transactions_partitions.rs fn app(servers: &str) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new([servers]).default_group("billing-svc"), |b| { // One transactional id per source partition: "billing-svc-1-p0", "billing-svc-1-p1". let lanes = Publish::default() .transactional_id("billing-svc-1") .per_partition(); let invoices = subscriber("invoice-batches", Bill) .map_source(|_| KafkaTopic::new("invoice-batches").commit(Commit::Tracked)) .workers_by_key(nonzero!(4)); b.include(invoices.build()).out(DefaultSlot, lanes).build(); }, ) }

This guide chooses what ack and nack commit on Kafka: librdkafka's own commits, precise at-least-once with Commit::Tracked, and batches settled element by element. Kafka does not settle single messages. A consumer group commits a position per partition, and everything below it counts as read. A handler still settles each delivery, so the subscription's Commit mode decides how those settlements become a position. Mode ack drop retry After a crash Auto (default) nothing nothing reports unsupported, the record does not come back the tail of handled records is read again, or records stored but not handled are skipped Tracked settles the offset settles the offset the record comes back every record not settled is read again Transactional settles the offset, committed with the pipeline's transaction the same as ack stalls the window until the transaction deadline the open window is read again The example is a payouts service: payouts must not be lost, page views may be. Transactions and exactly-once covers the third mode.

pay_out sends a payout through the bank and answers with a confirmation. When the bank does not answer, the payout comes back and is tried again. Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Payout { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "payouts.done")] struct Paid { payout_id: u64, } #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("payouts").commit(Commit::Tracked), reply)] async fn pay_out(payout: &Payout, State(bank): State<Arc<Bank>>) -> Result<Paid, HandlerOutcome> { if payout.amount_cents == 0 { return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } if bank.0.call().await.is_err() { tracing::warn!(payout.id, "bank unavailable, payout comes back"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } tracing::info!(payout.id, payout.amount_cents, "payout sent"); Ok(Paid { payout_id: payout.id, }) } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Payout { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Paid { payout_id: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Paid { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "payouts.done"; } impl MessageHeaders for Paid { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Paid { const NAME: &'static str = "Paid"; } struct PayOut; impl Handle<Payout, Paid, (), (), Clients> for PayOut { async fn handle( &self, payout: &Payout, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> Result<Paid, HandlerOutcome> { if payout.amount_cents == 0 { return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } if ctx.state().bank.call().await.is_err() { tracing::warn!(payout.id, "bank unavailable, payout comes back"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } tracing::info!(payout.id, payout.amount_cents, "payout sent"); Ok(Paid { payout_id: payout.id, }) } } Under Commit::Tracked an ack moves the committed position up to the lowest delivery that is still open. Acks from concurrent workers arrive out of order, and the position never passes a payout that is still in flight. retry hands the delivery back to its subscription, which delivers it again before anything it fetches next. Until then its offset stays open, so the position does not move past it. A process that stops first gets the payout back from Kafka when it starts again. So a payout is never lost, and it may be handled twice: once before a crash and once after. The bank call has to accept a repeated payout, for example by its id. A retry without an attempt cap comes back forever; Retries and dead-letter topics adds the cap.

count_view counts page views in an analytics store. A lost view does not matter here, so the subscription keeps the default mode. Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct PageView { page: String, } #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("page-views").group("analytics"))] async fn count_view(view: &PageView, State(counters): State<Arc<Counters>>) -> HandlerOutcome { if counters.0.call().await.is_err() { // Under `Commit::Auto` nothing brings the view back; analytics accepts the loss. return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::debug!(page = %view.page, "page view counted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct PageView { page: String, } struct CountView; impl Handle<PageView, (), (), (), Clients> for CountView { async fn handle( &self, view: &PageView, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if ctx.state().counters.call().await.is_err() { // Under `Commit::Auto` nothing brings the view back; analytics accepts the loss. return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } tracing::debug!(page = %view.page, "page view counted"); Ok(()) } } Under Commit::Auto librdkafka stores the position when it hands the record to the application and commits it on a timer. ack and drop change nothing. retry reports itself unsupported, and the view does not come back. This mode costs the least, and a crash can lose handled records or skip records that were stored but not handled.

reconcile takes statement lines in batches of up to 500 and settles each line on its own. Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct StatementLine { payout_id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("statements").group("reconciliation").commit(Commit::Tracked))] async fn reconcile(lines: &[StatementLine]) -> Vec<HandlerOutcome> { lines .iter() .map(|line| { if line.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(line.payout_id, "empty statement line dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() }) .collect() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct StatementLine { payout_id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } struct Reconcile; impl Handle<[StatementLine], (), (), (), Clients> for Reconcile { fn handle( &self, lines: &[StatementLine], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { if lines.iter().all(|line| line.amount_cents > 0) { return ready(Ok(())); } let outcomes = lines .iter() .map(|line| { if line.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(line.payout_id, "empty statement line dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() }) .collect(); ready(Err(outcomes)) } } A batch is one delivery plus the records librdkafka has already fetched, with no extra waiting, so it is often smaller than the size the mount site names. The returned list settles the batch element by element; in the manual form Ok(()) acks every element and Err(outcomes) settles each one. Under Commit::Tracked an element that asks for a retry comes back alone, and the committed position stops in front of it until it settles. A process that stops first reads the acked elements behind it again: duplicates, not loss. How much librdkafka keeps queued is a consumer property, set with KafkaTopic::config. When the queue is full, librdkafka pauses fetching for fetch.queue.backoff.ms (1000 ms by default), which slows large records behind a slow handler. .config("fetch.queue.backoff.ms", "10") shortens the pause.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = Clients> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]) .default_group("payouts") .producer_config("enable.idempotence", "true") .flush_timeout(Duration::from_secs(10)); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payouts", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Clients::default())) .with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(pay_out) .out_reply(Publish::default().queue_timeout(Duration::from_secs(5))); b.include(count_view); b.include(reconcile.batch(nonzero!(500usize))); }) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App<State = Clients> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]) .default_group("payouts") .producer_config("enable.idempotence", "true") .flush_timeout(Duration::from_secs(10)); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payouts", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Clients::default())) .with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber("payouts", PayOut) .map_source(|_| KafkaTopic::new("payouts").commit(Commit::Tracked)) .reply() .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish::default().queue_timeout(Duration::from_secs(5))); b.include( subscriber("page-views", CountView) .map_source(|_| KafkaTopic::new("page-views").group("analytics")) .build(), ); b.include( subscriber("statements", Reconcile) .batch(nonzero!(500usize)) .map_source(|_| { KafkaTopic::new("statements") .group("reconciliation") .commit(Commit::Tracked) }) .build(), ); }) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } At-least-once from end to end needs the producer side too. enable.idempotence makes librdkafka's own resends of a record land once; producer_config sets it and every other producer property, acks included. Every publish waits for the cluster's delivery report, so a publish that returned Ok was accepted by Kafka. A publish waits for space while librdkafka's local queue is full, which slows the handler down to what the cluster takes. queue_timeout bounds that wait and turns it into an error. At shutdown the broker flushes the records still in flight, for up to flush_timeout (30 seconds by default). ClosedKafkaBroker::unflushed_records counts the records that did not make it. The tests in the example file run the app in process and replace the bank and the analytics store with clients that fail once. The in-process Kafka commits as a cluster does, so the payout comes back under Commit::Tracked and the page view does not under Commit::Auto.

This guide publishes several records as one Kafka transaction, runs transactions under a worker pool, and makes a consume-transform-produce handler exactly-once. A Kafka transaction makes a set of records visible together. A reader at read_committed isolation, librdkafka's default, sees all of them once the transaction commits and none of them after an abort. In RustStream a transaction is a property of the publish policy at the mount site, and the handler names only the capability it uses.

ship turns a paid order into one shipment line per item. An order with an empty line is dropped, and none of its lines may reach the warehouse. Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Order { id: u64, items: Vec<Item>, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Item { sku: String, quantity: u32, } /// One shipment line per item of a paid order. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "shipment-lines")] struct ShipmentLine { order_id: u64, sku: String, quantity: u32, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(ShipmentLine)] struct Shipments; #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("paid-orders").group("shipping").commit(Commit::Tracked))] async fn ship( order: &Order, Out(shipments): Out<impl TransactionalPublisher, Shipments>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { if shipments.begin_transaction().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } for item in &order.items { if item.quantity == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, sku = %item.sku, "order with an empty line dropped"); return match shipments.abort().await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::drop(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), }; } let line = ShipmentLine { order_id: order.id, sku: item.sku.clone(), quantity: item.quantity, }; if shipments.message(&line).publish().await.is_err() { shipments.abort().await.ok(); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } } if shipments.commit().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(order.id, lines = order.items.len(), "order shipped"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, items: Vec<Item>, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Item { sku: String, quantity: u32, } /// One shipment line per item of a paid order. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct ShipmentLine { order_id: u64, sku: String, quantity: u32, } // `#[derive(Outgoing)]` with `#[outgoing(name = "shipment-lines")]`, by hand. impl OutgoingDestination for ShipmentLine { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "shipment-lines"; } impl MessageHeaders for ShipmentLine { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for ShipmentLine { const NAME: &'static str = "ShipmentLine"; const DESCRIPTION: Option<&'static str> = None; } /// The slot the shipment lines leave through. struct Shipments; impl OutSlot for Shipments { const NAME: &'static str = "Shipments"; // `ShipmentLine` fixes its destination, so no transform on this slot may name one. type Destination = Reads; } impl PublishedThrough<Shipments> for ShipmentLine {} struct Ship; impl<S> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(S,)>> for Ship where S: OutEntry<Shipments, Wire: TransactionalPublisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(S,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let shipments = outs.get(Shipments); if shipments.begin_transaction().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } for item in &order.items { if item.quantity == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, sku = %item.sku, "order with an empty line dropped"); return match shipments.abort().await { Ok(()) => Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()), Err(_) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()), }; } let line = ShipmentLine { order_id: order.id, sku: item.sku.clone(), quantity: item.quantity, }; if shipments.message(&line).publish().await.is_err() { shipments.abort().await.ok(); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } } if shipments.commit().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } tracing::info!(order.id, lines = order.items.len(), "order shipped"); Ok(()) } } The handler takes its slot as Out<impl TransactionalPublisher, Shipments>: it names the core's TransactionalPublisher capability and nothing of Kafka. Records published between begin_transaction and commit become visible together. abort discards them, so the first line of the order with an empty line never reaches a reader. Outside an open transaction the slot publishes like a plain one. A second begin_transaction while one is open reports KafkaError::TransactionBusy, and a commit or abort with nothing open reports KafkaError::NoTransaction. The transaction covers the published lines and not the consumed order. Commit::Tracked commits the order's offset after the handler acks it. A crash between the two delivers the order again and ships its lines a second time. The exactly-once pipeline below closes that gap.
documents.s: All or nothing from one handler

documents.t: One Kafka producer runs one transaction at a time, so the handlers of a worker pool cannot share one transactional publisher. invoice runs four lanes and gives each source partition a transaction of its own. Macros Manual src/main.rs /// One invoice line per item of a billed order. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "invoice-items")] struct InvoiceItem { order_id: u64, sku: String, quantity: u32, } #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("billable-orders").group("invoicing").commit(Commit::Tracked), workers(4, by_key) )] async fn invoice( order: &Order, Ctx(partition): Ctx<Partition>, Out(lanes): Out<impl PartitionLanes>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let Ok(items) = lanes.for_partition(partition).await else { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); }; if items.begin_transaction().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } for item in &order.items { let line = InvoiceItem { order_id: order.id, sku: item.sku.clone(), quantity: item.quantity, }; if items.message(&line).publish().await.is_err() { items.abort().await.ok(); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } } if items.commit().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(order.id, partition, "order invoiced"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// One invoice line per item of a billed order. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct InvoiceItem { order_id: u64, sku: String, quantity: u32, } impl OutgoingDestination for InvoiceItem { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "invoice-items"; } impl MessageHeaders for InvoiceItem { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for InvoiceItem { const NAME: &'static str = "InvoiceItem"; const DESCRIPTION: Option<&'static str> = None; } /// Declaring `KafkaContext` is what gives the body the delivery's partition. struct Invoice; impl<L> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(L,)>, KafkaContext> for Invoice where L: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: PartitionLanes>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(L,)>, ctx: &mut Context<'_, KafkaContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let partition = ctx.context(Partition); let Ok(items) = outs.get(DefaultSlot).for_partition(partition).await else { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); }; if items.begin_transaction().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } for item in &order.items { let line = InvoiceItem { order_id: order.id, sku: item.sku.clone(), quantity: item.quantity, }; if items.message(&line).publish().await.is_err() { items.abort().await.ok(); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } } if items.commit().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } tracing::info!(order.id, partition, "order invoiced"); Ok(()) } } workers(4, by_key) keys the lanes by partition, so one partition is handled in order on one lane. The slot is PartitionLanes: for_partition returns the transactional publisher of the delivery's partition, created on its first use. Lanes that handle different partitions run their transactions at the same time. The transactional ids follow the topic's partitions, not the number of workers, so changing workers(n) changes no id. This scheme needs the default lane key. LaneKey::RecordKey spreads one partition across several lanes, which would then share one partition's publisher and collide on its single transaction.

enrich reads a placed order and answers with the totals the warehouse plans with. Each answer is published exactly once, even when the service crashes and the order is read again. Macros Manual src/main.rs /// A placed order with the totals the warehouse plans with. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "enriched-orders")] struct EnrichedOrder { id: u64, lines: usize, units: u32, } #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("placed-orders") .group("enrichment") .commit(Commit::Transactional("enrichment-1".into())), reply, workers(4, by_key) )] async fn enrich(order: &Order) -> EnrichedOrder { let units = order.items.iter().map(|item| item.quantity).sum(); tracing::info!(order.id, units, "order enriched"); EnrichedOrder { id: order.id, lines: order.items.len(), units, } } src/main.rs /// A placed order with the totals the warehouse plans with. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct EnrichedOrder { id: u64, lines: usize, units: u32, } impl OutgoingDestination for EnrichedOrder { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "enriched-orders"; } impl MessageHeaders for EnrichedOrder { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for EnrichedOrder { const NAME: &'static str = "EnrichedOrder"; const DESCRIPTION: Option<&'static str> = None; } struct Enrich; impl Handle<Order, EnrichedOrder> for Enrich { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<EnrichedOrder, HandlerOutcome>> { let units = order.items.iter().map(|item| item.quantity).sum(); tracing::info!(order.id, units, "order enriched"); ready(Ok(EnrichedOrder { id: order.id, lines: order.items.len(), units, })) } } The handler only returns its reply; it holds no transaction code. Commit::Transactional("enrichment-1") stops the subscription from committing offsets on its own. The pipeline of the same id commits them instead, inside the transaction that carries the replies. So the consumed position and the published records move together: either both commit, or neither does.

The mount site names the policy behind each slot and reply. Macros Manual src/main.rs fn service(broker: KafkaBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("fulfilment", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // One transactional id per service instance. b.include(ship) .out(Shipments, Publish::default().transactional_id("shipping-1")) .build(); // One transactional id per source partition: "invoicing-1-p0", "invoicing-1-p1", ... b.include(invoice) .out( DefaultSlot, Publish::default() .transactional_id("invoicing-1") .per_partition(), ) .build(); // The pipeline's id is the one the subscription's commit mode names. b.include(enrich) .out_reply(EosPublish::new("enrichment-1")) .transform(EosReplies); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { service(KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"])) } src/main.rs fn service(broker: KafkaBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("fulfilment", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // One transactional id per service instance. let paid = subscriber("paid-orders", Ship).map_source(|_| { KafkaTopic::new("paid-orders") .group("shipping") .commit(Commit::Tracked) }); b.include(paid.build()) .out(Shipments, Publish::default().transactional_id("shipping-1")) .build(); // One transactional id per source partition: "invoicing-1-p0", "invoicing-1-p1", ... let billable = subscriber("billable-orders", Invoice) .map_source(|_| { KafkaTopic::new("billable-orders") .group("invoicing") .commit(Commit::Tracked) }) .workers_by_key(nonzero!(4)); b.include(billable.build()) .out( DefaultSlot, Publish::default() .transactional_id("invoicing-1") .per_partition(), ) .build(); // The pipeline's id is the one the subscription's commit mode names. let placed = subscriber("placed-orders", Enrich) .map_source(|_| { KafkaTopic::new("placed-orders") .group("enrichment") .commit(Commit::Transactional("enrichment-1".into())) }) .reply() .workers_by_key(nonzero!(4)); b.include(placed.build()) .out_reply(EosPublish::new("enrichment-1")) .transform(EosReplies); }) } fn app() -> impl App { service(KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"])) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } transactional_id turns the plain policy into a transactional one. One transactional id belongs to one live producer: a second producer that starts with the same id fences the first, and the first can no longer commit. Give every running instance of the service its own id, for example from the pod's ordinal. per_partition makes the id a base: the publishers of invoice take the ids invoicing-1-p0, invoicing-1-p1 and so on. EosPublish::new("enrichment-1") is the pipeline, and its id is the one the subscription's commit mode names. EosReplies carries each delivery's source position onto its reply, which is how the pipeline pairs the two. Without it the first reply fails instead of leaving outside the transaction.

The pipeline collects replies into a window and commits it every commit_interval, 100 ms unless set. At the end of a window it waits for every delivery that published into it to settle, adds their positions and the group's metadata to the transaction, and commits. So a reply becomes visible at least one commit interval after the handler returned it. A failed publish, a failed commit or a delivery that does not settle in time aborts the window. The consumers then seek back to the last committed offsets, and the whole window is handled again in a fresh transaction. The committed output still holds each reply once. The pipeline limits what its handlers can return and how they read: A retry() from a handler holds its window open until the transaction timeout, 30 seconds unless transaction_timeout sets another, and then the window replays. retry_after does not belong in a pipeline handler: its delayed copy is published outside the window and breaks the pairing of records and offsets. KafkaPartitions does not combine with Commit::Transactional, and such a subscription fails to start: the pipeline commits through the consumer group, and a reader of fixed partitions takes no part in one.
This guide installs ruststream-rdkafka, starts a local Kafka and runs a first service against it.

Cargo.toml [dependencies] ruststream = { version = "0.7", features = ["macros", "json", "logging"] } ruststream-rdkafka = "0.7" serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] } tracing = "0.1" [dev-dependencies] ruststream-rdkafka = { version = "0.7", features = ["testing"] } tokio = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt"] } ruststream is the framework: macros gives the attributes, json the default codec, and logging prints the service's log to the terminal. ruststream-rdkafka is the Kafka broker. Its testing feature adds the in-process Kafka that tests run on. The broker crate has these features: Feature What it gives json (default), msgpack, cbor the codec of the same name schema-registry the Confluent Schema Registry client and its wire format avro Avro over the Schema Registry protobuf Protobuf messages, with the Confluent envelope asyncapi the Kafka bindings in the generated AsyncAPI document testing the in-process Kafka behind TestApp ssl TLS through the system OpenSSL ssl-vendored TLS through an OpenSSL built from source zstd the zstd compression codec

The crate builds librdkafka, the C client of Kafka, from source. The build needs a C compiler and make; librdkafka configures itself with its own script. On Debian and Ubuntu, build-essential provides both. The ssl feature also needs the OpenSSL headers (libssl-dev), and ssl-vendored needs perl to build OpenSSL. A CMake build or a system librdkafka is a feature of rust-rdkafka: add rdkafka to your own dependencies with the feature you need, and the build picks it up.

One Kafka node in KRaft mode is enough to develop against: compose.yaml services: kafka: image: apache/kafka:4.0.0 ports: - "9092:9092" Start it and create the topic the service reads: docker compose up -d docker compose exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh \ --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic orders The broker listens on localhost:9092.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber("orders")] async fn take_order(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("orders-svc"), |b| { b.include(take_order); }, ) } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } struct TakeOrder; impl Handle<Order> for TakeOrder { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("orders-svc"), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", TakeOrder).build()); }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } take_order reads JSON orders from the orders topic. It acknowledges an order with an amount and drops one without. KafkaBroker::new takes the bootstrap servers and only records them. The connection opens when the service starts. Kafka reads a topic only inside a consumer group. default_group is the group of every subscription that names none. #[ruststream::app] turns app into main; in the manual form, run_main does the same. Run the service: cargo run -- run Publish an order from another terminal with the console producer that ships in the image: echo '{"id":1,"amount_cents":1250}' | docker compose exec -T kafka \ /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic orders The service logs order taken with the order's id. Ctrl+C stops it. cargo generate scaffolds the same kind of service with a router and a reply: cargo generate --git https://github.com/powersemmi/ruststream-rdkafka templates/kafka-topic --name my-service

The example file also holds two tests. Each starts the same app with TestApp::start, publishes an order and checks how take_order settled it. KafkaBroker connects to an in-process Kafka there, so the tests need no cluster: cargo test Testing a Kafka service walks through these tests and what the in-process Kafka models.

A service on rust-rdkafka writes its own consumer loop and producer. Here is where each part goes in RustStream: rust-rdkafka RustStream ClientConfig::new().set("group.id", ..) default_group, or KafkaTopic::group per subscription ClientConfig::set for any other property KafkaBroker::config, producer_config, KafkaTopic::config StreamConsumer::subscribe and a recv loop a #[subscriber] handler deserializing message.payload() the handler's parameter type, decoded by the codec store_offset or commit_message after the work Commit::Tracked and the handler's outcome (Commits and delivery guarantees) FutureProducer::send a reply or an Out parameter, sent through a publish policy seek and assign start_at at the mount site, or the seek handle in the handler (Replay and seeking) send_offsets_to_transaction EosPublish (Transactions and exactly-once)

This guide reads a topic in consumer groups, keeps the order of each key with parallel lanes, and places records on partitions by key, by number or in turn. The example is a bank's ledger service. It posts transfers to account ledgers, screens them for fraud, keeps an index of its records and opens cases for disputed transfers.

Kafka keeps the order of records inside one partition. Records with the same key land on the same partition, so the order of each key holds. post reads transfers keyed by account and handles up to eight at once without breaking that order. Macros Manual src/main.rs /// The account a record belongs to, carried as the Kafka record key. #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize)] struct AccountKey { #[serde(rename = "kafka-partition-key")] account: String, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Transfer { id: u64, amount_cents: i64, } /// One line of an account's ledger, keyed by the account like the transfer it came from. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "bank.entries", headers = AccountKey)] struct Entry { transfer_id: u64, amount_cents: i64, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Entry)] struct Entries; #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("transfers").lane_key(LaneKey::RecordKey), workers(8, by_key) )] async fn post( transfer: &Transfer, Headers(key): Headers<AccountKey>, Out(entries): Out<impl Publisher, Entries>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let entry = Entry { transfer_id: transfer.id, amount_cents: transfer.amount_cents, }; if entries .message(&entry) .with_headers(&key) .publish() .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(transfer.id, account = %key.account, "transfer posted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// The account a record belongs to, carried as the Kafka record key. #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct AccountKey { #[serde(rename = "kafka-partition-key")] account: String, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Transfer { id: u64, amount_cents: i64, } /// One line of an account's ledger, keyed by the account like the transfer it came from. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Entry { transfer_id: u64, amount_cents: i64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Entry { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "bank.entries"; } impl MessageHeaders for Entry { type Contract = WithHeaders<AccountKey>; } impl MessageInfo for Entry { const NAME: &'static str = "Entry"; } struct Entries; impl OutSlot for Entries { const NAME: &'static str = "Entries"; type Destination = Reads; } impl PublishedThrough<Entries> for Entry {} struct Post; impl<Ledger> Handle<Message<AccountKey, Transfer>, (), Outs<(Ledger,)>> for Post where Ledger: OutEntry<Entries, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, transfer: &Message<AccountKey, Transfer>, outs: &Outs<(Ledger,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let key = &transfer.headers; let entry = Entry { transfer_id: transfer.body.id, amount_cents: transfer.body.amount_cents, }; if outs .get(Entries) .message(&entry) .with_headers(key) .publish() .await .is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } tracing::info!(transfer.body.id, account = %key.account, "transfer posted"); Ok(()) } } workers(8, by_key) runs eight lanes; deliveries with the same lane key run one after another on one lane. LaneKey::RecordKey keys the lanes by the record key, so two transfers of one account never run at the same time, even inside one partition. The default, LaneKey::Partition, keys them by the source partition, which also covers records without a key. In the manual form the same setting is workers_by_key. The record key reaches the handler as the kafka-partition-key header (PARTITION_KEY_HEADER). AccountKey is a header contract with one field under that name. Headers<AccountKey> reads the key of the delivery, and with_headers(&key) writes it as the key of the ledger entry. So the entry goes to the partition of its account in bank.entries too, and readers of the ledger see each account in order. A transfer without a key fails the header contract and is settled by the decode policy, which drops it by default.

A consumer group reads each record once, whichever of its members gets the partition. Every group reads its own copy. screen reads the same transfers in a group of its own, so it sees every transfer that post sees. Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("transfers") .group("fraud-check") .start(StartOffset::Earliest) .assignment(Assignment::CooperativeSticky) )] async fn screen(transfer: &Transfer) -> HandlerOutcome { if transfer.amount_cents > 1_000_000 { tracing::warn!(transfer.id, "large transfer flagged"); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs struct Screen; impl Handle<Transfer> for Screen { fn handle( &self, transfer: &Transfer, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if transfer.amount_cents > 1_000_000 { tracing::warn!(transfer.id, "large transfer flagged"); } ready(Ok(())) } } KafkaTopic::group names the group. A subscription that names none joins the broker's default_group; post does. Kafka reads a topic only inside a group, so a service with neither fails at startup. StartOffset says where a group starts when it has no committed offset for a partition. That is the case on its first run and after retention deleted its offset. Earliest starts at the oldest record, Latest at the end of the log, and the default Committed leaves the choice to librdkafka's auto.offset.reset, which is latest. Assignment picks how the group shares partitions among its members. CooperativeSticky moves only the partitions that change owner when a member joins or leaves, so the others keep running. Startup waits until the group has assigned this member its partitions, up to assignment_timeout (60 seconds by default). After that, every record published to the topic reaches the subscription. Give each subscription of a service its own group. Two subscriptions of different topics in one group rebalance each other: when the second joins, the first loses its partitions for a moment. The first member reads nothing until the group has assigned the partitions again, and then continues where it stopped.

KafkaTopics reads several topics through one consumer and one group. KafkaTopics::pattern reads every topic whose name matches a regular expression, which must start with ^. archive reads every topic of the bank and records where each record sits. A pinned partition wins over the record key, and the record key wins over librdkafka's partitioner. A partition the topic does not have fails the publish.

A record with a key or a pinned partition keeps its placement. The count is fixed: it matches the partitions the cycle should use, never more than the topic has. A subscription over a set of topics has no single topic to send a retry copy to, so the app names one with ToSourceTopic; Retries and dead-letter topics explains it. The tests in the example file run the app in process. The in-process Kafka gives every topic one partition, so the test of placement on several partitions runs against a cluster: KAFKA_TEST_URL=localhost:9092 cargo test
A production cluster asks for authentication and TLS, and a service sets its producer's durability and its own timeouts.

src/main.rs /// Where the cluster is and who the service is, as the deployment provides them. struct Cluster { servers: String, username: String, password: String, } impl Cluster { fn from_env() -> Self { let read = |name: &str| env::var(name).unwrap_or_default(); Self { servers: read("KAFKA_SERVERS"), username: read("KAFKA_USERNAME"), password: read("KAFKA_PASSWORD"), } } } fn broker(cluster: Cluster) -> KafkaBroker { KafkaBroker::new([cluster.servers]) .default_group("orders-svc") .config("security.protocol", "SASL_SSL") .config("sasl.mechanism", "SCRAM-SHA-512") .config("sasl.username", cluster.username) .config("sasl.password", cluster.password) .producer_config("acks", "all") .producer_config("enable.idempotence", "true") .connect_timeout(Duration::from_secs(10)) .flush_timeout(Duration::from_secs(20)) } Cargo.toml [dependencies] ruststream-rdkafka = { version = "0.7", features = ["ssl"] } The deployment provides the address and the credentials in environment variables. Every librdkafka property goes through KafkaBroker::config, which applies it to the consumers and the producer. security.protocol selects SASL over TLS, and sasl.mechanism the SASL mechanism. TLS needs librdkafka built with OpenSSL: the ssl feature links the system OpenSSL, and ssl-vendored builds one from source. SCRAM and OAUTHBEARER need the same feature, because librdkafka builds them on OpenSSL. SASL PLAIN over SASL_PLAINTEXT needs no feature. Kerberos (GSSAPI) is the gssapi feature of rust-rdkafka: add rdkafka to your dependencies with that feature. A cluster with TLS and no SASL takes security.protocol set to SSL, and the ssl.* properties name the certificates.

producer_config sets a property on the producer only. acks=all makes the cluster confirm a record once every in-sync replica has it. enable.idempotence keeps a producer retry from writing a record twice. Every publish waits for the cluster's confirmation, so a successful publish means the cluster accepted the record. The broker has timeouts of its own: connect_timeout bounds the check that the cluster is reachable at startup. flush_timeout bounds the flush of unsent records at shutdown. assignment_timeout bounds how long startup waits for the group to assign a subscription its partitions.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("orders").commit(Commit::Tracked), reply)] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); Confirmation { id: order.id } } fn service(broker: KafkaBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(confirm) .out_reply(Publish::default().queue_timeout(Duration::from_secs(5))); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { service(broker(Cluster::from_env())) } src/main.rs struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); ready(Ok(Confirmation { id: order.id })) } } fn service(broker: KafkaBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber("orders", Confirm) .map_source(|_| KafkaTopic::new("orders").commit(Commit::Tracked)) .reply() .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish::default().queue_timeout(Duration::from_secs(5))); }) } fn app() -> RustStream { service(broker(Cluster::from_env())) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } A publish waits for space in librdkafka's local queue when the queue is full. queue_timeout on the publish policy turns a longer wait into an error. A subscription sets its own properties with KafkaTopic::config, and they win over the broker's. Two properties belong to the commit mode: enable.auto.commit and enable.auto.offset.store. Under Commit::Tracked and Commit::Transactional a subscription that sets either refuses to start, and the error names the property and the mode.

The tests start the production service with the production broker, given test credentials, under TestApp::start. The in-process Kafka validates the configuration the way librdkafka does, without dialling the cluster. A property name or value that librdkafka refuses fails the start with librdkafka's message: Invalid value "SASL_TLS" for configuration property "security.protocol" The tests need the same features as the service. librdkafka built without OpenSSL refuses SASL_SSL and SSL as values of security.protocol. Authentication itself happens only on a real cluster.

This guide handles prost-generated Protobuf messages that carry the Confluent envelope: it reads framed records without a registry and publishes framed replies. A registry-backed Protobuf record starts with the Confluent envelope: a zero byte, the four-byte schema id, and a message-index path that names which message of the schema follows. A generated message is not a serde type, so it does not go through a codec. It encodes and decodes itself, and the broker puts the envelope on and takes it off. Cargo.toml [dependencies] ruststream-rdkafka = { version = "0.7", features = ["protobuf"] } prost = "0.14" Use the prost version the crate depends on.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// What `prost-build` generates for `shipping.Parcel`, plus the decode lane. #[derive(Clone, PartialEq, prost::Message, Deserialized)] #[wire(decode = decode_confluent)] struct Parcel { #[prost(int64, tag = "1")] id: i64, #[prost(string, tag = "2")] address: String, } /// What `prost-build` generates for `shipping.Label`, plus the encode lane and its topic. #[derive(Clone, PartialEq, prost::Message, Serialized, Outgoing)] #[wire(encode = ::prost::Message::encode)] #[outgoing(name = "labels")] struct Label { #[prost(int64, tag = "1")] parcel: i64, #[prost(string, tag = "2")] address: String, } src/main.rs /// What `prost-build` generates for `shipping.Parcel`. #[derive(Clone, PartialEq, prost::Message)] struct Parcel { #[prost(int64, tag = "1")] id: i64, #[prost(string, tag = "2")] address: String, } // The decode lane: the envelope is stepped over, then `prost` reads the message. impl Deserialized for Parcel { type Output<'a> = Self; type Error = KafkaError; fn from_payload(payload: &[u8]) -> Result<Self, Self::Error> { decode_confluent(payload) } } impl Input for Parcel { type Axis = SoloDeserialized<Self>; } /// What `prost-build` generates for `shipping.Label`. #[derive(Clone, PartialEq, prost::Message)] struct Label { #[prost(int64, tag = "1")] parcel: i64, #[prost(string, tag = "2")] address: String, } // The encode lane: `prost` writes the message into the publish buffer. impl Serialized for Label { type Error = prost::EncodeError; fn wire_bytes(&self, buf: &mut BytesMut) -> Result<WireBytes<'_>, Self::Error> { prost::Message::encode(self, &mut *buf)?; Ok(WireBytes::InBuffer) } } impl MessageWire for Label { type Wire = SerializedWire; } impl ReplyShape for Label { type Body = Self; type Headers = (); type Wire = SerializedReply; } // What `#[derive(Outgoing)]` with `#[outgoing(name = "labels")]` writes. impl OutgoingDestination for Label { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "labels"; } impl MessageHeaders for Label { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Label { const NAME: &'static str = "Label"; const DESCRIPTION: Option<&'static str> = None; } Parcel and Label are what prost-build generates from this schema, plus the derives of RustStream: shipping.proto syntax = "proto3"; package shipping; message Parcel { int64 id = 1; string address = 2; } message Label { int64 parcel = 1; string address = 2; } In a build script, prost-build's message_attribute adds the derives to the generated structs. #[derive(Deserialized)] lets a handler take the message, and #[derive(Serialized)] lets it return one. #[wire(..)] names the function that reads or writes the bytes. In the manual form, the impls take the place of the derives. Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber("parcels", reply)] async fn print_label(parcel: &Parcel) -> Result<Label, HandlerOutcome> { if parcel.address.is_empty() { tracing::warn!(parcel.id, "parcel without an address dropped"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } tracing::info!(parcel.id, "label printed"); Ok(Label { parcel: parcel.id, address: parcel.address.clone(), }) } src/main.rs struct PrintLabel; impl Handle<Parcel, Label> for PrintLabel { fn handle( &self, parcel: &Parcel, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Label, HandlerOutcome>> { if parcel.address.is_empty() { tracing::warn!(parcel.id, "parcel without an address dropped"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(parcel.id, "label printed"); ready(Ok(Label { parcel: parcel.id, address: parcel.address.clone(), })) } } print_label takes the generated Parcel and returns the generated Label. A parcel with no address is dropped, and nothing is published for it.

decode_confluent is the decode function of Parcel. It steps over the envelope and the message-index path, then prost reads the message. It needs no registry: the generated type already knows its fields. A record with no envelope is read as a bare message, so a topic where some producers frame and others do not still decodes.

Macros Manual src/main.rs fn service(broker: KafkaBroker, registry: &SchemaRegistry) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(print_label) .out_reply(KafkaPublish::framed(registry)); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { service( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("shipping-svc"), &SchemaRegistry::new("http://localhost:8081"), ) } src/main.rs fn service(broker: KafkaBroker, registry: &SchemaRegistry) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber("parcels", PrintLabel).reply().build()) .out_reply(KafkaPublish::framed(registry)); }) } fn app() -> impl App { service( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("shipping-svc"), &SchemaRegistry::new("http://localhost:8081"), ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } Label writes bare Protobuf, and the publish policy puts the envelope in front of it. KafkaPublish::framed is that policy, named for the reply with out_reply. On the first publish to a topic, it looks up the topic's subject (labels-value) and caches its schema id. The index path defaults to the schema's first message. message names another message for a topic, and subject another subject. The subject is resolved on the first publish, not at startup, because the topic is only known then. When the registry does not hold the subject, or holds another format there, the publish fails and the delivery settles as a retry. With the default commit mode a retry is not redelivered; Commits and delivery guarantees covers the modes. ProtobufFrame frames for a whole app, added with RustStream::publish_layer. It frames what leaves through Out slots and publishers the mount sites do not name, when the destination subject holds a Protobuf schema, and passes the rest through as it is. A reply goes straight to its own publisher and does not pass through the layer, so a replying handler names KafkaPublish::framed. A payload that already carries an envelope is left alone, so the layer and the policy combine.

Reading needs no registry, so print_label reads framed records under TestApp::start with no registry and no cluster. The example's first test publishes a framed parcel with no address and checks that it is dropped and that no label is published. A framed publish needs the subject's schema id, so the tests of the label run against a registry. Testing a Kafka service covers the harness.

A Protobuf schema cannot be derived from a generated type. So the .proto source is registered separately, with SchemaRegistry::register and SchemaType::Protobuf, or with the registry's own tools. The schema registered for a framed topic may import only the well-known types (google/protobuf/*.proto); other schema references are not resolved.

This guide reads a topic again from the start or from a moment, and moves a running subscription from inside its handler. Kafka keeps the log after a consumer has read it. A service can read it again: to rebuild a read model, to backfill a new consumer, or to skip records it cannot use. A subscription takes its start position at the mount site, and a handler moves its own subscription through the delivery's context.

The service keeps two read models in memory: the balance of every account and the spend of every card. Each posting carries the ledger's revision. A correction of past postings is published as a new revision, and a read model that meets one rebuilds itself from the start of the log. Macros Manual src/main.rs /// One posting of the ledger. `revision` is the ledger's revision: a correction of past /// postings is published as a new revision, and a read model meeting one rebuilds itself. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Entry { id: u64, account: String, amount_cents: i64, revision: u32, } /// A read model kept in memory: the balance of every account. #[derive(Debug, Default)] struct Projection { revision: u32, balances: HashMap<String, i64>, } impl Projection { /// Applies `entry`, or clears the model and answers `false` when the entry belongs to a newer /// revision, which the model has to be rebuilt for from the start of the log. fn apply(&mut self, entry: &Entry) -> bool { if entry.revision > self.revision { self.revision = entry.revision; self.balances.clear(); return false; } *self.balances.entry(entry.account.clone()).or_default() += entry.amount_cents; true } } /// The service's state: one read model per subscription that builds one. #[derive(Clone, Default)] struct Projections { balances: Arc<Mutex<Projection>>, spend: Arc<Mutex<Projection>>, } src/main.rs /// One posting of the ledger. `revision` is the ledger's revision: a correction of past /// postings is published as a new revision, and a read model meeting one rebuilds itself. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Entry { id: u64, account: String, amount_cents: i64, revision: u32, } /// A read model kept in memory: the balance of every account. #[derive(Debug, Default)] struct Projection { revision: u32, balances: HashMap<String, i64>, } impl Projection { /// Applies `entry`, or clears the model and answers `false` when the entry belongs to a newer /// revision, which the model has to be rebuilt for from the start of the log. fn apply(&mut self, entry: &Entry) -> bool { if entry.revision > self.revision { self.revision = entry.revision; self.balances.clear(); return false; } *self.balances.entry(entry.account.clone()).or_default() += entry.amount_cents; true } } /// The service's state: one read model per subscription that builds one. #[derive(Clone, Default)] struct Projections { balances: Arc<Mutex<Projection>>, spend: Arc<Mutex<Projection>>, }

The balances live in memory, so after a restart they are built again from the whole log. Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("ledger").group("balances").commit(Commit::Tracked), start_at(KafkaPosition::earliest()) )] async fn project_balance( entry: &Entry, ctx: &mut Context<'_, KafkaContext, Projections>, Ctx(seeker): Ctx<SeekHandle>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let applied = ctx .state() .balances .lock() .unwrap_or_else(PoisonError::into_inner) .apply(entry); if applied { tracing::info!(entry.id, "balance updated"); return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } tracing::info!( entry.id, entry.revision, "new revision, rebuilding the balances" ); if seeker.seek(KafkaPosition::earliest()).await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// Declaring `KafkaContext` is what puts the seek handle in the context. struct ProjectBalance; impl Handle<Entry, (), (), KafkaContext, Projections> for ProjectBalance { async fn handle( &self, entry: &Entry, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, KafkaContext, Projections>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let applied = ctx .state() .balances .lock() .unwrap_or_else(PoisonError::into_inner) .apply(entry); if applied { tracing::info!(entry.id, "balance updated"); return Ok(()); } tracing::info!( entry.id, entry.revision, "new revision, rebuilding the balances" ); if ctx .context(SeekHandle) .seek(KafkaPosition::earliest()) .await .is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } start_at(KafkaPosition::earliest()) opens the subscription at the start of the log on every start, whatever the group balances committed before. StartOffset on the descriptor differs here: it applies only while the group has no committed offset. The position lands on the partitions the group assigns to this consumer, before their first record. KafkaPosition has five positions: Position Where the subscription resumes earliest() the oldest record Kafka keeps latest() the end of the log, so only new records are read offset(partition, n) offset n of one partition topic_offset(topic, partition, n) offset n of one partition of one topic, for a subscription that reads several topics timestamp(ms) the first record stamped at or after ms, in every partition A start position that names none of the subscription's partitions fails the start. Under Assignment::CooperativeSticky the first assignment may be only part of the group's share, and partitions that arrive in a later increment are not moved.

The same handler rebuilds the balances when a posting of a newer revision arrives. Ctx<SeekHandle> gives the handler the KafkaSeeker of its own subscription. seek moves the subscription to the start of the log, and the handler reads every posting again. The posting that started the rebuild comes back as well, and this time the projection applies it. A seek takes any of the positions above. Ctx<Position> holds the delivery's own position: a seek there reads the record again, and everything after it. Ctx<Partition> and Ctx<Offset> give the coordinates for an offset(..) position.

Card postings arrive in volume, so the spend is built in batches of up to 500. Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("card-entries") .group("card-spend") .commit(Commit::Tracked))] async fn project_spend( entries: &[Entry], ctx: &mut Context<'_, KafkaBatchContext, Projections>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let applied = { let mut spend = ctx .state() .spend .lock() .unwrap_or_else(PoisonError::into_inner); entries.iter().all(|entry| spend.apply(entry)) }; if applied { tracing::info!(entries = entries.len(), "card spend updated"); return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } tracing::info!("new revision, rebuilding the card spend"); if ctx .context(SeekHandle) .seek(KafkaPosition::earliest()) .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// A batch body declares `KafkaBatchContext`, which carries the same seek handle. struct ProjectSpend; impl Handle<[Entry], (), (), KafkaBatchContext, Projections> for ProjectSpend { async fn handle( &self, entries: &[Entry], _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, KafkaBatchContext, Projections>, ) -> Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>> { let applied = { let mut spend = ctx .state() .spend .lock() .unwrap_or_else(PoisonError::into_inner); entries.iter().all(|entry| spend.apply(entry)) }; if applied { tracing::info!(entries = entries.len(), "card spend updated"); return Ok(()); } tracing::info!("new revision, rebuilding the card spend"); if ctx .context(SeekHandle) .seek(KafkaPosition::earliest()) .await .is_err() { return Err(entries.iter().map(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()).collect()); } Ok(()) } } A batch handler declares KafkaBatchContext instead of the per-delivery context. It carries the same SeekHandle key and no position, because a batch spans many records. The subscription moves once the whole batch has settled.

The payout review reads the payouts of the last seven days on every start. Macros Manual src/main.rs /// A payout as the payments service publishes it. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Payout { id: u64, amount_cents: i64, } #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("payouts") .group("payout-review") .commit(Commit::Tracked))] async fn review_payout(payout: &Payout) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(payout.id, payout.amount_cents, "payout reviewed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// A payout as the payments service publishes it. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Payout { id: u64, amount_cents: i64, } /// The body reads no context, but runs in an app whose state is `Projections`. struct ReviewPayout; impl Handle<Payout, (), (), (), Projections> for ReviewPayout { fn handle( &self, payout: &Payout, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Projections>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(payout.id, payout.amount_cents, "payout reviewed"); ready(Ok(())) } } The moment is known only when the service starts, so the mount site names the position instead of the attribute. b.include(project_spend.batch(nonzero!(500usize))); b.include(review_payout.start_at(KafkaPosition::timestamp(epoch_millis(review_from)))); }) } /// The review reads the payouts of the last seven days on every start. const REVIEW_WINDOW: Duration = Duration::from_hours(7 * 24); b.include( subscriber("card-entries", ProjectSpend) .map_source(|_| { KafkaTopic::new("card-entries") .group("card-spend") .commit(Commit::Tracked) }) .batch(nonzero!(500usize)) .build(), ); b.include( subscriber("payouts", ReviewPayout) .map_source(|_| { KafkaTopic::new("payouts") .group("payout-review") .commit(Commit::Tracked) }) .start_at(KafkaPosition::timestamp(epoch_millis(review_from))) .build(), );
