service(KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]), review_from) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } KafkaPosition::timestamp takes milliseconds since the epoch, the unit Kafka stamps records with. Kafka resolves the moment in each partition to the first record stamped at or after it. A partition with no such record resumes at its end.

A seek moves this consumer, not the group. It moves the partitions this member holds and commits nothing for anyone. Other members of the group keep reading where they are. The next rebalance discards the seek: whoever gets a partition then resumes from the group's committed offset. A start_at position applies again at every start.
documents.s: What a seek does to the group

documents.t: All three subscriptions commit with Commit::Tracked (Commits and delivery guarantees). A seek clears the tracked position of every partition it moves. A delivery pulled before the seek settles into nothing, so the ack of the posting that started the rebuild commits nothing. A later commit therefore never passes a record that the seek replayed and no handler has handled yet.

This guide retries a Kafka record now or later, caps the attempts and moves what keeps failing to a dead-letter topic, on one topic or several. Kafka does not hold a record back and does not count deliveries. The framework does both: the mount site declares the cap and the dead-letter topic, and a retry travels as a copy of the record with a retry count in a header. The example is a refunds service that sends refunds through a card processor.

The processor refuses a refund in three ways, and each needs a different outcome. Busy means its rate limit is used up: a retry right now would be refused again, so retry_after waits 30 seconds. Unavailable means it did not answer: retry tries again at once. Declined means the card account is closed, and another try gets the same answer, so the refund is dropped. Macros Manual src/main.rs /// How long a busy processor asks its callers to wait. const BACKOFF: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] struct Refund { id: u64, card: String, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("refunds").commit(Commit::Tracked))] async fn process_refund( refund: &Refund, State(processor): State<Arc<Processor>>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { settle(&processor, refund).await } async fn settle(processor: &Processor, refund: &Refund) -> HandlerOutcome { match processor.refund(refund).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), // Past the rate limit: a delivery right now would be refused again. Err(Refusal::Busy) => HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF), // No answer: try again at once, up to the attempt cap. Err(Refusal::Unavailable) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), Err(Refusal::Declined) => { tracing::warn!(refund.id, "card declined, refund dropped"); HandlerOutcome::drop() } } } src/main.rs /// How long a busy processor asks its callers to wait. const BACKOFF: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Refund { id: u64, card: String, amount_cents: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Refund { type Form = CallerName; } impl MessageHeaders for Refund { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Refund { const NAME: &'static str = "Refund"; } struct ProcessRefund; impl Handle<Refund, (), (), (), Clients> for ProcessRefund { async fn handle( &self, refund: &Refund, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { settle(&ctx.state().processor, refund).await } } async fn settle(processor: &Processor, refund: &Refund) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { match processor.refund(refund).await { Ok(()) => Ok(()), // Past the rate limit: a delivery right now would be refused again. Err(Refusal::Busy) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF)), // No answer: try again at once, up to the attempt cap. Err(Refusal::Unavailable) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()), Err(Refusal::Declined) => { tracing::warn!(refund.id, "card declined, refund dropped"); Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()) } } } retry_after settles the record and publishes a copy back to refunds once the delay has passed. The copy carries the retry-count header (RETRY_COUNT_HEADER), raised by one. The delayed copy is at-most-once: a process that stops before the delay ends loses it. The copy is a new record at the end of the topic, so the records behind the refund do not wait for it. retry under a declared cap also becomes a copy, published at once. Without a cap it hands the record back to the subscription under Commit::Tracked, as Commits and delivery guarantees shows.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = Clients> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("refunds", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Clients::default())) .with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("refunds"), |b| { // Five deliveries of one refund, the first included; then the dead-letter topic. b.include(process_refund) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("refunds.dlq"); b.include(review); // A set of topics names where a copy goes: back to the topic it came from. b.include(process_regional_refund) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("refunds.dlq") .out_retry(Publish::default()) .transform(ToSourceTopic); }, ) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App<State = Clients> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("refunds", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Clients::default())) .with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("refunds"), |b| { // Five deliveries of one refund, the first included; then the dead-letter topic. b.include( subscriber("refunds", ProcessRefund) .map_source(|_| KafkaTopic::new("refunds").commit(Commit::Tracked)) .build(), ) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("refunds.dlq"); b.include( subscriber("refunds.dlq", Review) .map_source(|_| { KafkaTopic::new("refunds.dlq") .group("refunds-review") .start(StartOffset::Earliest) }) .build(), ); // A set of topics names where a copy goes: back to the topic it came from. b.include( subscriber("refunds.eu,refunds.us", ProcessRegionalRefund) .map_source(|_| { KafkaTopics::new(["refunds.eu", "refunds.us"]) .group("regional-refunds") .commit(Commit::Tracked) }) .build(), ) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("refunds.dlq") .out_retry(Publish::default()) .transform(ToSourceTopic); }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } max_attempts counts every delivery of one refund, the first included. The fifth delivery is not retried: dead_letter publishes it to refunds.dlq, payload and headers as they arrived. A dropped refund settles and goes nowhere; the dead-letter topic holds only the refunds that ran out of attempts. Retry and dead-letter topics are the service's infrastructure: create them like any other topic, and the framework only publishes to them.
documents.s: The cap and the dead-letter topic

documents.t: The dead-letter topic is an ordinary topic, and review reads it like any other. Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("refunds.dlq") .group("refunds-review") .start(StartOffset::Earliest) )] async fn review(refund: &Refund, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let deliveries = ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("1"); tracing::error!(refund.id, deliveries, "refund needs a person to look at it"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs struct Review; impl Handle<Refund, (), (), (), Clients> for Review { fn handle( &self, refund: &Refund, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let deliveries = ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("1"); tracing::error!(refund.id, deliveries, "refund needs a person to look at it"); ready(Ok(())) } } The retry-count header of a dead-lettered record holds the number of deliveries it went through, 5 here. review reads it with ctx.headers() and logs the refund for a person to look at.

A copy of a record is published to the topic the subscription reads. KafkaTopic reads one topic, so it needs nothing more. KafkaTopics and KafkaPartitions read a set that no single publish reaches, so their registration names where a copy goes, and the service refuses to start without it. Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber( KafkaTopics::new(["refunds.eu", "refunds.us"]) .group("regional-refunds") .commit(Commit::Tracked) )] async fn process_regional_refund( refund: &Refund, Ctx(topic): Ctx<Topic>, State(processor): State<Arc<Processor>>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::debug!(refund.id, %topic, "regional refund"); settle(&processor, refund).await } src/main.rs struct ProcessRegionalRefund; impl Handle<Refund, (), (), KafkaContext, Clients> for ProcessRegionalRefund { async fn handle( &self, refund: &Refund, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, KafkaContext, Clients>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { tracing::debug!(refund.id, topic = %ctx.context(Topic), "regional refund"); settle(&ctx.state().processor, refund).await } } The app mounts process_regional_refund with .out_retry(Publish::default()).transform(ToSourceTopic). ToSourceTopic sends each copy back to the topic its delivery came from, so a retried refund from refunds.us comes back on refunds.us. It reads the topic from the Kafka context, so the handler takes a context key such as Ctx<Topic>; in the manual form its context type is KafkaContext. .out_retry(Publish::default()).to("refunds.retry") sends every copy to one topic of your own instead; list that topic in the subscription so the copies come back. The same rule holds for a subscription that never retries: every registration over a set of topics names a retry destination.
The tests in the example file run the app in process with a paused clock, so tb.advance(BACKOFF) lets the 30 seconds pass at once. Testing a Kafka service covers the harness.

This guide reads and writes Avro and JSON Schema records under the Confluent envelope, with every schema checked against the Schema Registry at startup. A registry-backed record starts with the Confluent envelope: a zero byte, then the four-byte id of the schema it was written with. The schemas themselves live in the registry. In RustStream the schema belongs to the codec, so handlers take and return plain serde structs. Cargo.toml [dependencies] ruststream-rdkafka = { version = "0.7", features = ["avro"] } apache-avro = { version = "0.22", features = ["derive"] } The avro feature adds the Avro codec on top of schema-registry, which brings the registry client and the envelope. apache-avro provides the AvroSchema derive; use the version the crate depends on.
documents.s: Schema Registry: Avro and JSON Schema

documents.t: Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, AvroSchema)] struct Invoice { id: i64, amount_cents: i64, // Added in the second version of the schema; older producers do not write it. #[avro(default = r#""EUR""#)] currency: String, } #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, AvroSchema, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] struct Receipt { invoice: i64, amount_cents: i64, currency: String, } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, AvroSchema, JsonSchema)] struct Invoice { id: i64, amount_cents: i64, // Added in the second version of the schema; older producers do not write it. #[avro(default = r#""EUR""#)] currency: String, } #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, AvroSchema, JsonSchema)] struct Receipt { invoice: i64, amount_cents: i64, currency: String, } // What `#[derive(Outgoing)]` with `#[outgoing(name = "receipts")]` writes. impl OutgoingDestination for Receipt { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "receipts"; } impl MessageHeaders for Receipt { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Receipt { const NAME: &'static str = "Receipt"; const DESCRIPTION: Option<&'static str> = None; } AvroSchema derives each struct's Avro schema. currency arrived in the second version of the invoice schema. #[avro(default)] is the value a record written without it reads as.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber("invoices", reply)] async fn issue_receipt(invoice: &Invoice) -> Receipt { tracing::info!(invoice.id, invoice.amount_cents, "receipt issued"); Receipt { invoice: invoice.id, amount_cents: invoice.amount_cents, currency: invoice.currency.clone(), } } src/main.rs struct IssueReceipt; impl Handle<Invoice, Receipt> for IssueReceipt { fn handle( &self, invoice: &Invoice, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(invoice.id, invoice.amount_cents, "receipt issued"); ready(Ok(Receipt { invoice: invoice.id, amount_cents: invoice.amount_cents, currency: invoice.currency.clone(), })) } } issue_receipt reads an invoice and answers with a receipt on the receipts topic. Nothing in it knows about Avro or the envelope.

Macros Manual src/main.rs fn service(broker: KafkaBroker, registry: SchemaRegistry) -> impl App { let prefetch = SchemaPrefetch::new(registry); let avro = AvroCodec::registry(&prefetch) .register::<Receipt>("receipts-value") .resolve_onto(Invoice::get_schema()) .expect("a registry codec resolves its reader schema on the first delivery"); let json = SchemaFramed::new(&prefetch, JsonCodec); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker_codec( broker.schema_prefetch(prefetch), avro.clone(), |b| { b.include(issue_receipt) .out_reply(KafkaPublish::default()) .codec(avro); b.include_router(Router::new().with_codec(json).include(open_dispute)); }, ) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { service( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("billing-svc"), SchemaRegistry::new("http://localhost:8081"), ) } src/main.rs fn service(broker: KafkaBroker, registry: SchemaRegistry) -> impl App { let prefetch = SchemaPrefetch::new(registry); let avro = AvroCodec::registry(&prefetch) .register::<Receipt>("receipts-value") .resolve_onto(Invoice::get_schema()) .expect("a registry codec resolves its reader schema on the first delivery"); let json = SchemaFramed::new(&prefetch, JsonCodec); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker_codec( broker.schema_prefetch(prefetch), avro.clone(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("invoices", IssueReceipt).reply().build()) .out_reply(KafkaPublish::default()) .codec(avro); b.include_router( Router::new() .with_codec(json) .include(subscriber("disputes", OpenDispute).build()), ); }, ) } fn app() -> impl App { service( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("billing-svc"), SchemaRegistry::new("http://localhost:8081"), ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } SchemaRegistry::new records the registry's URL and sends nothing yet. Every clone of it shares one cache, so a schema is fetched once per process. SchemaPrefetch does the network work, and schema_prefetch attaches it to the broker. When the broker connects, the prefetch resolves every subject the codecs publish under. When a record arrives, it fetches the writer schema the envelope names, before the codec runs. So the codec itself never waits on the network. AvroCodec::registry builds the Avro codec from the prefetch. register names the subject a type's values are framed under: receipts go out under receipts-value. Decoding needs no registration, since each record names its own writer schema. with_broker_codec decodes every handler of the scope with the Avro codec. A reply is encoded with the codec named at its mount site, and with the default JSON codec when none is named. So out_reply(KafkaPublish::default()).codec(avro) names the Avro codec for the receipts.
documents.s: The registry, the prefetch and the codec

documents.t: resolve_onto makes Avro resolve every record onto the reader schema, here Invoice::get_schema(). A record written under the first version of the schema has no currency. Resolution fills it from the field's default, so the handler reads "EUR". A reader schema applies to every record its codec decodes, so a codec with one serves one type. A second type with its own reader schema gets its own codec, in its own router.

The service registers no schemas: whoever owns a topic registers its subject, for example in a deploy step. register_avro registers a type's Avro schema under a subject, register_json its JSON Schema, and register a schema given as text. When a subject a codec publishes under is not in the registry, the broker does not connect, and the error names the subject. MissingSubject chooses what happens instead: Policy What it does Refuse (default) the service does not start AutoRegister registers the type's own schema under the subject, and logs a warning PublishUnframed publishes the bare datum with no envelope, and logs a warning Set it with on_missing_subject before the codecs are built from the prefetch.
documents.s: Registering subjects and a missing subject

documents.t: At connect, each registered type's schema is checked the way registering it would be checked. The subject's compatibility level decides which versions it is checked against: the latest one, or every version under a _TRANSITIVE level. A model that drifted from its subject stops the service, and the registry's account of the difference is in the error. check_compatibility(false) turns the check off, for a subject whose level is NONE.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct Dispute { invoice: i64, reason: String, } #[subscriber("disputes")] async fn open_dispute(dispute: &Dispute) -> HandlerOutcome { if dispute.reason.is_empty() { tracing::warn!(dispute.invoice, "dispute without a reason dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(dispute.invoice, dispute.reason, "dispute opened"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct Dispute { invoice: i64, reason: String, } struct OpenDispute; impl Handle<Dispute> for OpenDispute { fn handle( &self, dispute: &Dispute, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if dispute.reason.is_empty() { tracing::warn!(dispute.invoice, "dispute without a reason dropped"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(dispute.invoice, dispute.reason, "dispute opened"); ready(Ok(())) } } SchemaFramed wraps the core's JSON codec in the envelope. Decoding steps over the envelope and reads the JSON document inside it. Encoding frames a value with the id of the subject that register names for its type, as with Avro. In the service above, a router gives the disputes subscription this codec, since the most specific codec wins. JsonSchema derives the type's JSON Schema, which register_json registers.

Macros Manual src/main.rs fn archive(broker: KafkaBroker) -> impl App { let pinned = AvroCodec::local(Invoice::get_schema()).expect("the invoice schema resolves"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing-archive", "0.1.0")).with_broker_codec( broker, pinned, |b| { b.include(archive_invoice); }, ) } #[subscriber("invoices.archive")] async fn archive_invoice(invoice: &Invoice) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(invoice.id, "invoice archived"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs fn archive(broker: KafkaBroker) -> impl App { let pinned = AvroCodec::local(Invoice::get_schema()).expect("the invoice schema resolves"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing-archive", "0.1.0")).with_broker_codec( broker, pinned, |b| { b.include(subscriber("invoices.archive", ArchiveInvoice).build()); }, ) } struct ArchiveInvoice; impl Handle<Invoice> for ArchiveInvoice { fn handle( &self, invoice: &Invoice, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(invoice.id, "invoice archived"); ready(Ok(())) } } AvroCodec::local holds one schema and uses it for every record. The topic carries the bare Avro datum: no envelope, no registry and no network on the path. This archive service therefore runs, and is tested, without a registry.

A service can also keep plain serde models on the default JSON codec and convert at the broker's edges. KafkaBroker::schema_registry converts every framed delivery to JSON before the codec runs. SchemaFrame, added with RustStream::publish_layer, frames each outgoing JSON payload in the format its destination subject holds: Avro, JSON Schema or Protobuf. A topic with no subject in the registry is published as it is. This path costs a JSON conversion per message, and it does not resolve records onto a reader schema. A broker uses one path or the other: with schema_registry attached, a codec would be handed JSON.

SchemaRegistry::with_client takes a RegistryClient of your own, such as one over another HTTP stack or another client crate. The codecs, the prefetch and the transcode path then reach the registry through it. A crate that does the whole schema work itself, such as schema_registry_converter, works on bytes instead. The handler takes the record's bytes through a #[derive(Deserialized)] type and returns the encoded reply through a #[derive(Serialized)] type. Only bytes cross between that crate and RustStream, so its own apache-avro version does not have to match this crate's.

A test runs the service's own app with TestApp, against an in-process Kafka or against a cluster. The service under test charges card payments. A payment arrives on card-payments, and its record key is the account to charge. The handler replies with a receipt on card-receipts. A payment without a key is dropped. A payment over the bank's instant limit is held: the handler asks for it again in a minute with retry_after. After three deliveries a payment goes to card-payments.review, the dead-letter topic. The app is built by service(broker), so a test chooses the broker and main uses the production one. The tests need the testing feature of ruststream-rdkafka in [dev-dependencies].

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_keyed_payment_gets_a_receipt() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("payments-svc"); let tb = TestApp::start(service(broker)).await?; a_receipt_names_the_account_of_the_key(tb).await } async fn a_receipt_names_the_account_of_the_key(tb: TestApp<()>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let mut key = HeaderMap::new(); key.insert(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, "acct-7"); tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>() .message(&Payment { id: 1, amount_cents: 2_500, }) .with_headers(key) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("card-receipts") .assert_called_once() .with(&Receipt { payment: 1, account: "acct-7".to_owned(), }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_keyed_payment_gets_a_receipt() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("payments-svc"); let tb = TestApp::start(service(broker)).await?; a_receipt_names_the_account_of_the_key(tb).await } async fn a_receipt_names_the_account_of_the_key(tb: TestApp<()>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let mut key = HeaderMap::new(); key.insert(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, "acct-7"); tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>() .message(&Payment { id: 1, amount_cents: 2_500, }) .with_headers(key) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("card-receipts") .assert_called_once() .with(&Receipt { payment: 1, account: "acct-7".to_owned(), }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } TestApp::start connects KafkaBroker to an in-process Kafka. The bootstrap address is never dialled. The test addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>(). A Kafka record key travels as the PARTITION_KEY_HEADER header, so the test sets it with with_headers. The broker turns that header into the record's native key, and the handler reads it back with Ctx<Key>. publish returns once the handler and its reply have settled. So the next lines assert on finished state: how the subscriber settled and what reached card-receipts. The body takes the started app as an argument, so the live test below runs it too.

documents.t: The in-process Kafka reads the configuration librdkafka would read: the broker's config and producer_config, each descriptor's options, and librdkafka's defaults. A property librdkafka refuses fails the test's start the same way. It models Kafka rather than a queue: Each consumer group reads a record once, and every group reads its own copy. The commit mode decides what is committed: a retry under Commit::Tracked comes back, and under Commit::Auto it reports itself unsupported. A record key places the record and comes back to the handler. A seek moves a subscription to an offset, either end of the log, or a timestamp. A read_committed reader sees a transaction's records when it commits and never after an abort. Every topic has one partition there. Several partitions, cooperative rebalancing, retention and the timing of a real group join need a cluster.

Its deadline is the longest a publish waits for the reaction to settle; a real cluster needs more than the in-process default. The test reads the address from KAFKA_TEST_URL with live::url, a helper of the example's own, and skips when it is unset. It joins a consumer group of its own, so nothing an earlier run left behind is read. It creates card-payments first: a subscription opens on the partitions a topic has, and a topic that appears later is read from where auto.offset.reset puts it. The assertions are the in-process ones, unchanged. cargo test KAFKA_TEST_URL=localhost:9092 cargo test -- --test-threads=1
